# team reviews it; the two optional roles are bound to this app's helpers.

files.examples/ember-app/enola/recipes/ember-c:
recipe: ember-conventions
roles:
  - name: components
    match: ["app/components/**"]
  - name: integration-tests
    kind: test_ref
    match: ["tests/integration/**"]
  - name: actions
    kind: symbol
    where: { decorators: action }
  - name: framework-controllers
    kind: symbol
    where: { superclass_module: "@ember/controller" }
  - name: constructors
    match: ["app/**"]
    name_pattern: "*.constructor"
  - name: fetchers
    match: ["app/services/**"]
  - name: legacy-accessor
    match: ["app/utils/**"]
    name_pattern: "*.get"
  - name: argument-mutators
    kind: symbol
    where: { fields_written: args }
  - name: element-modifiers
    kind: symbol
    match: ["app/components/**", "app/modifiers/**"]
  - name: state-writing-members
    kind: symbol
    where: { fields_written: "<any>" }
  - name: task-factories
    optional: true
  - name: fixture-setup
    optional: true
rules:
  - id: no-action-decorator
    forbid_fact: actions
    because: "An arrow function binds lexically and needs no decorator; the decorator predates it and the convention says to stop writing it."

  - id: no-framework-controllers
    forbid_fact: framework-controllers
    because: "A route component replaces the controller and its template. Controllers are quirky and carry surprising singleton state, and the convention is to stop adding them."

  - id: components-import-no-render-modifiers
    forbid: components
    to_name: ["@ember/render-modifiers*", "ember-render-helpers*"]
    via: imports
    because: "The render-helper form fires on a lifecycle rather than attaching to the element it acts on, and it has been discouraged for years. A named modifier attaches to the element and says what it acts on."

  - id: constructors-do-not-fetch
    forbid: constructors
    to: fetchers
    via: calls
    because: "Rendering pulls data in as it is needed. A constructor that fetches is eager, runs before anything asks, and cannot be re-run when the arguments change."

  - id: no-legacy-property-accessor
    forbid: components
    to: legacy-accessor
    via: calls
    because: "The proxy accessor reads through a layer that no longer exists on a resolved value, and it defeats type checking. Reach for the property."

  - id: arguments-are-not-mutated
    forbid_fact: argument-mutators
    because: "Data flows down and actions flow up. A component that writes through its own arguments changes state it does not own, and the owner never learns of it. Pass a callback and let the owner make the change."

  - id: a-modifier-takes-its-element
    require: element-modifiers
    when_edge_to: ["*.modifier"]
    via: calls
    must_prop_contain: { prop: takes_parameters, value: "yes" }
    because: "A modifier is handed the element it is attached to. One that declares no parameter is not modifying anything; it is a side effect fired by render, and a getter or a tracked task says that honestly."

  - id: derivations-do-not-write
    forbid: state-writing-members
    to: task-factories
    via: calls
    because: "A task is derived state and runs inside the render cycle. Writing the component's own state from one schedules another render off the render it is running in. Return the data and read it through the task's value instead."

  - id: component-tests-carry-no-fixtures
    forbid: integration-tests
    to: fixture-setup
    via: calls
    because: "A fixture library sets up back-end state and has no place in a component test: if the component makes no request, build a front-end record, and if it does, let the acceptance layer answer it."

# A Go service

A chi service in four layers, small enough to read in a minute, that
breaks its laws on purpose. [Guide 17](../../guides/17-go.md) walks
through it.

| Layer | Directory |
|---|---|
| presentation | `internal/web` |
| application | `internal/checkout` |
| domain | `internal/order` |
| infrastructure | `internal/store` |

The laws are in `enola/constraints/`: the `layered` recipe bound to the
four directories, the domain's law over `imports` (the recipe's own domain
rules read `depends_on`, which this language's extractor does not write),
and the `supply-chain` recipe. What breaks:

- `shop/presentation-reaches-application-only`: `internal/web/routes.go` (`listRecent` reads the store).
- `the-domain-imports-no-storage`: `internal/order/pricing.go` (imports the store).

`supply-chain` is bound and holds: a `require` in `go.mod` names an exact version.

```bash
cd examples/go-service
enola --generate .
enola constraints lint .
```

The breaches are findings in `.enola/insights.json` with source
`constraints`. `EXPECTED` lists the rule ids that must report one, and
`script/test-examples` fails when the set changes.
files.examples/go-service/enola/constraints/do:
# layered's domain rules read depends_on, an edge the Go extractor does
# not write; an import is the edge a domain package crosses to reach storage.
components:
  - name: domain
    match: ["internal/order/**"]
  - name: storage
    match: ["internal/store/**"]
rules:
  - id: the-domain-imports-no-storage
    forbid: domain
    to: storage
    via: imports
    mode: ratchet
    because: "The domain is the part that outlives the database; a domain package that imports the store cannot be tested or reasoned about without it."

    bind:
      unpinned-dependencies: {}

# A knowledge base with enola, minimal

The smallest knowledge base that gets what [guide 09](../../guides/09-a-knowledge-base-with-enola.md) describes:
two pages anchored to code with `enola_intent`, a cluster config, the
committed receipts, and the finding ledger. The skills under
[`templates/skills`](../../templates/skills) and the hooks under
[`templates/hooks`](../../templates/hooks) run against exactly these
files.

- `enola-cluster.yaml`: the members, the knowledge base among them.
- `wiki/shop/permanent/architecture.md`: a page whose `enola_intent`
  anchors it to `app/jobs/**` and `app/models/**`, with one receipt
  citation.
- `wiki/shop/permanent/public-surface.md`: a page anchored to the
  controllers it describes.
- `wiki/_state/enola/receipts.json`: what `kb enola generate` recorded.
- `wiki/_state/enola/findings.json`: the ledger, one judged finding.

`governing_intent app/jobs/order_mailer_job.rb` returns the first page;
`kb enola citations` verifies its citation against the receipts file. The
`kb` wrapper is [`templates/kb/kb`](../../templates/kb/kb)
(`enola-guides copy templates/kb` writes it to `bin/kb`); run it from this
directory. enola labels each member by its directory name, so the
receipts are keyed `rails-shop` and `ember-app`.

Four rings. An entity that calls a use case and a use case that calls an
adapter both point outward; the controller calling inward is the direction the
arrangement allows. The shipped clean recipe names the two outward reaches.

# cluster laws

Laws that only a cluster snapshot can answer: a table owned by two
repositories, mutating actions selected through the routes they handle, and
routes no loaded client calls. Each refuses by name in a single-repository
snapshot rather than reporting silence as compliance.

One file per law under `enola/constraints/`, each file declaring the parts it speaks about. Copy it, run `enola constraints lint .`,
then `enola --generate . && enola constraints ledger .` for each law's
count of breaches. With a baseline pinned before the copy (`enola baseline pin .`),
`enola check .` lists each breach under `Newly declared`.
files.examples/laws/cluster-laws/enola/constra:
Enola.architecture "platform" do
  part :mutating_actions, service: :backend, files: "app/controllers/**", handles: [:post, :put, :patch, :delete]
  part :policies, service: :backend, files: "app/policies/**"

  law "a mutating action is authorized" do
    mutating_actions.must_reach :policies
    why "an action behind a POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE route changes state, and the policy call is the one place the change is authorized"
    mode :advisory
  end
end

Enola.architecture "platform" do
  part :api, service: :backend, files: "config/**", kind: :route

  law "every api route has a consumer" do
    api.must_have_consumer
    why "a route nobody calls is a surface nobody maintains"
    mode :advisory
  end
end

Enola.architecture "platform" do
  part :tables, files: "app/models/**", kind: :storage

  law "one owner per table" do
    tables.must_be_unique_across by: :table
    why "a table two repositories both model is written by two codebases that never see each other's validations or callbacks"
    mode :advisory
  end
end

# foreign keys

A foreign-key law reads the storage facts the schema yields: every table
carrying a tenant column must declare the foreign key to the tenant table. The
require form verdicts what a member fact carries, with a when antecedent
narrowing to the tables the law is about, so a table without the column is
never asked.

Declaration under `enola/constraints/`. Copy it, run `enola constraints lint .`,
then `enola --generate . && enola constraints ledger .` for each law's
count of breaches. With a baseline pinned before the copy (`enola baseline pin .`),
`enola check .` lists each breach under `Newly declared`.
files.examples/laws/foreign-keys/enola/constra:
components:
  - name: tables
    match: ["db/structure.sql", "db/schema.rb", "app/models/**"]
    kind: storage

rules:
  - id: account-fk
    require: tables
    when_prop_contains: { prop: columns, value: account_id }
    must_prop_contain: { prop: fk_constraints, value: "account_id->accounts" }
    mode: advisory
    because: "A table carrying account_id references an account, so the database should say so with a foreign key. Advisory while a backfill path that ships the column before the constraint is reconciled with the rule; the verdict names every table that carries the column without the key."

# instantiation

What Ruby code constructs, as a fact. `new` on a literal constant is an
instantiates relation from the calling member to the class, which is the one
call whose result has a knowable type; `new` on a variable receiver names no
class and records nothing. A construction whose result is immediately sent a
message is the one-shot ceremony, named on the calling member as Class.method,
so a component can select the members that perform it and a rule can forbid
it. A construction bound to a local first is not the ceremony.

Declaration: `enola/constraints/ceremony.yaml`.

Verify it on your own tree: copy `enola/` into the repository, run
`enola constraints lint .`, then `enola --generate . && enola constraints ledger .` for each law's
count of breaches. With a baseline pinned before the copy (`enola baseline pin .`),
`enola check .` lists each breach under `Newly declared`.

# maintenance tasks

Two laws for a maintenance-tasks directory: a naming convention the runner
depends on, and a boundary against controller code that has no request to
read. Both were mined from a codebase where they already held, which is the
right moment to declare a law.

One file per law under `enola/constraints/`, each file declaring the parts it speaks about. Copy it, run `enola constraints lint .`,
then `enola --generate . && enola constraints ledger .` for each law's
count of breaches. With a baseline pinned before the copy (`enola baseline pin .`),
`enola check .` lists each breach under `Newly declared`.
files.examples/laws/maintenance-tasks/enola/co:
Enola.architecture "app" do
  part :tasks, files: "app/tasks/**"
  part :controllers, files: "app/controllers/**"

  law "a maintenance task never invokes controller code" do
    tasks.must_not_call controllers
    why "a task runs from the runner or the console with no request around it, so controller code reached from one has nothing to read"
  end
end

Enola.architecture "app" do
  part :maintenance_tasks, files: "app/tasks/**", kind: :symbol, where: { symbol_kind: "class" }

  law "every maintenance task lives in the Maintenance namespace" do
    maintenance_tasks.names_must_match "Maintenance::*"
    why "the task runner resolves task constants from that namespace, so a task declared outside it never appears in the runner and cannot be run by anyone"
  end
end

A module never reaches the classes that include it. Taggable calls Post, which
includes it; Auditable calls Ledger, which does not. Who includes whom comes
from the resolved ancestry the rubydex provider emits, so the rule refuses
with a named cause on a snapshot without it and names Taggable on one with it.

# one door

A boundary with one sanctioned crossing: controllers may not reach the GraphQL
schema, except the single execute action, named as an exemption with its owner
and reason so the carve-out is a decision and not a hole.

Declaration under `enola/constraints/`. Copy it, run `enola constraints lint .`,
then `enola --generate . && enola constraints ledger .` for each law's
count of breaches. With a baseline pinned before the copy (`enola baseline pin .`),
`enola check .` lists each breach under `Newly declared`.
files.examples/laws/one-door/enola/constraints:
components:
  - name: controllers
    match: ["app/controllers/**"]
  - name: schema
    match: ["app/graphql/**"]

rules:
  - id: controllers-reach-the-schema-through-one-door
    forbid: controllers
    to: schema
    via: calls
    mode: advisory
    exempt:
      - witness: "Api::GraphqlController#execute -> AppSchema.execute via calls"
        owner: platform
        since: "2026-08-22"
        because: "the one sanctioned entry point"
    because: "Controllers reach the schema through exactly one door, the execute action; every other controller stays out of it. A second door is a second place to forget authentication."

Parts that may not depend on each other in a circle. Jobs reach models and
models reach jobs, so the two form a cycle at the part level; mailers sit
downstream of models only. The rule contracts the module graph to one node per
declared part, admits the symbol-rollup edges Ruby has, and names the circle;
the downstream part is not in it.

Declaration: `enola/constraints/cycles.yaml`.

Verify it on your own tree: copy `enola/` into the repository, run
`enola constraints lint .`, then `enola --generate . && enola constraints ledger .` for each law's
count of breaches. With a baseline pinned before the copy (`enola baseline pin .`),
`enola check .` lists each breach under `Newly declared`.
files.examples/laws/parts-never-cycle/enola/co:

  - name: jobs
    match: ["app/jobs/**"]
  - name: models
    match: ["app/models/**"]
  - name: mailers
    match: ["app/mailers/**"]
rules:
  - id: parts-never-cycle
    forbid_cycles: jobs
    among: [models, mailers]
    because: "parts that reach each other in a circle cannot be taken apart"

can read at the file level, so a component names the files that are its public
surface; reaching a public file from outside is fine and reaching an internal
one is the breach.

# rails forbidden names

A naming convention phrased as a prohibition. require_name demands a pattern
and has no negative, so "no get_ prefixes on a model's public surface" could
not be declared. forbid_name takes the same bounded pattern dialect, tries it
against a method's bare name after its owner, and with surface: exported
judges the public surface only: the exported get_total is the breach, the
private get_lines is not the convention's surface, and total is outside the
pattern.

Verify it on your own tree: copy `enola/` into the repository, run
`enola constraints lint .`, then `enola --generate . && enola constraints ledger .` for each law's
count of breaches. With a baseline pinned before the copy (`enola baseline pin .`),
`enola check .` lists each breach under `Newly declared`.

# rails mutations are authorized

The code behind a mutating route is selected by the route's method through the
handled_by edge the Rails binder draws, and must reach a policy. create does
and update does not; index handles a GET and is never asked. The handles key
is what lets the law speak about routes without naming a single action.

Declaration: `enola/constraints/authorization.rb`.

Verify it on your own tree: copy `enola/` into the repository, run
`enola constraints lint .`, then `enola --generate . && enola constraints ledger .` for each law's
count of breaches. With a baseline pinned before the copy (`enola baseline pin .`),
`enola check .` lists each breach under `Newly declared`.

Enola.architecture "shop" do
  part :mutating_actions, files: "app/controllers/**", handles: [:post, :put, :patch, :delete]
  part :policies, files: "app/policies/**"

  law "a mutating action is authorized" do
    mutating_actions.must_reach :policies
    why "every write passes a policy before it touches a record"
  end
end

# readers read the store only

The allow form: a part's calls may land only in the named parts. Here readers
that must stay replayable may reach the store and nothing else.

then `enola --generate . && enola constraints ledger .` for each law's

components:
  - name: readers
    match: ["internal/readers/**"]
  - name: store
    match: ["internal/store/**"]

rules:
  - id: readers-read-the-store-only
    allow: readers
    only: [store]
    via: calls
    mode: advisory
    because: "A reader derives its answer from the store alone, which is what keeps every reader replayable against a snapshot; a reader that reaches anything else answers differently on a different machine."

# resolved ancestry

Ancestry a provider resolved, and a component selected by it. `superclass:`
reads the parent as the source spelled it, one level, so a class written as
`Base` inside `module Billing` is never seen as an ApplicationRecord. The
rubydex provider emits each class's linearised ancestor chain as resolved
implements edges, and `ancestor: ApplicationRecord` selects the grandchild
through them, so a rule over the hierarchy judges the hierarchy. Without the
provider the selector is refused with a named cause rather than holding
vacuously, which is what the channels lacking the provider score.

Verify it on your own tree: copy `enola/` into the repository, run
`enola constraints lint .`, then `enola --generate . && enola constraints ledger .` for each law's
count of breaches. With a baseline pinned before the copy (`enola baseline pin .`),
`enola check .` lists each breach under `Newly declared`.

# routes have consumers

A law across repositories refuses by name inside one. require_consumer asks
whether a client elsewhere in the cluster calls each route; a single-
repository snapshot cannot answer, so the rule emits the named refusal and no
verdict, which is the whole point: a route with no client in a snapshot that
loaded no clients must not read as unconsumed.

# storage stays home

A part keeps to the tables it owns. Billing reaches its own invoices table and
the orders table the orders part owns; only the second is a breach, named with
the table, and the cut names the orders part's public member that already
reaches the model. The storage facts come from the Rails model extraction, so
the law reads what the graph measured rather than a list someone wrote.

# A Python service

A FastAPI service in four layers, small enough to read in a minute, that
breaks its laws on purpose. [Guide 15](../../guides/15-python.md) walks
through it.

| Layer | Directory |
|---|---|
| presentation | `shop/api` |
| application | `shop/services` |
| domain | `shop/domain` |
| infrastructure | `shop/repositories` |

The laws are in `enola/constraints/`: the `layered` recipe bound to the
four directories, the domain's law over `imports` (the recipe's own domain
rules read `depends_on`, which this language's extractor does not write),
and the `supply-chain` recipe. What breaks:

- `shop/presentation-reaches-application-only`: `shop/api/orders.py` (`list_recent` reads a repository).
- `the-domain-imports-no-storage`: `shop/domain/pricing.py` (imports a repository).
- `supply/dependencies-are-pinned`: `fastapi>=0.110` in `pyproject.toml`, a range with no lockfile.

```bash
cd examples/python-service
enola --generate .
enola constraints lint .
```

The breaches are findings in `.enola/insights.json` with source
`constraints`. `EXPECTED` lists the rule ids that must report one, and
`script/test-examples` fails when the set changes.
files.examples/python-service/enola/constraint:
# layered's domain rules read depends_on, an edge Python's extractor does
# not write; an import is the edge a Python domain crosses to reach storage.
components:
  - name: domain
    match: ["shop/domain/**"]
  - name: storage
    match: ["shop/repositories/**"]
rules:
  - id: the-domain-imports-no-storage
    forbid: domain
    to: storage
    via: imports
    mode: ratchet
    because: "The domain is the part that outlives the database; a domain that imports a table cannot be tested or reasoned about without it."

# Every direct dependency pinned, or resolved by a lockfile enola reads.
use_recipe:
  - recipe: supply-chain
    as: supply
    mode: ratchet
    bind:
      unpinned-dependencies: {}

# What enola is, and the words these guides use

enola builds a graph of a codebase (modules, symbols, routes, tables,
dependencies, and the edges between them), keeps it as a snapshot, and
grades a change by comparing the snapshot before it with the snapshot
after it. It reports what the change did: a dependency cycle that now
spans four files, a job that started calling a controller, a second part
writing a table that was one part's own. Those are invisible to a tool
that reads one file at a time, and a report of everything already wrong
with a repository buries them; a report of what one change added does
not.

Read this page once, then [start here](01-start-here.md). Every term
below links to the guide that covers it.

## How the pieces fit

1. **Extractors** read the source, one per language, and write **facts**:
   one line per module, symbol, route, table or dependency, and one per
   edge between them (`imports`, `calls`, `depends_on`, `reads`, ...).
2. **Providers** add facts no extractor measures: Ruby's own resolution
   of constants and ancestry, a linter's results, a capture of the app at
   run time.
3. The facts of one run are a **snapshot**, written to `.enola/` with a
   **receipt** saying which extractors and providers ran and what they
   skipped.
4. **Explainers** read the snapshot and compute **findings**: cycles,
   layer violations, dead code, query loops, coupling hotspots, and the
   breaches of your laws. Each carries a confidence between 0 and 1.
5. A **baseline** is a snapshot pinned as "before". `enola check`
   compares the current snapshot with it and prints a **verdict**: the
   findings the change introduced and resolved, and whether any of them
   fails the build under the policy you set.

## Glossary

| Term | What it means here | Covered in |
|---|---|---|
| **fact** | One measured thing (a module, a symbol, a route, a table, a dependency) or one edge between two. A snapshot is a file of them, `.enola/facts.jsonl`. | [Start here](01-start-here.md#3-take-the-first-snapshot) |
| **extractor** | The part of enola that reads one language's source and writes its facts. Every language in the tree is indexed into one graph; there is nothing to configure. | [Start here](01-start-here.md#2-look-before-you-configure) |
| **provider** | A program enola runs beside its extractors to add facts they cannot measure. `rubydex` and `prism` are built into the binary; anything else is an executable you configure. | [Providers](07-providers.md) |
| **census** | The one line a provider prints about what it read and what it skipped, kept in the receipt. | [Providers](07-providers.md#the-census) |
| **receipt** | `.enola/receipt.json`: which extractors and providers produced a snapshot, at which versions, and what they skipped. Two snapshots with different receipts may not be comparable. | [Start here](01-start-here.md#3-take-the-first-snapshot) |
| **explainer** | A named analysis over the snapshot (`cycles`, `layers`, `dead-code`, `query-loops`, `constraints`, ...) that produces findings. `enola check --help` lists them; they are what `-fail-on` names. | [Reading a verdict](20-reading-a-verdict.md) |
| **finding** | One thing an explainer reports, with a confidence. Below 1.00 it is a candidate to verify, not a verdict. | [Reading a verdict](20-reading-a-verdict.md) |
| **baseline** | The snapshot a change is graded against. `enola baseline pin .` pins the current one; in CI the template grades against the pull request's merge-base. | [Start here](01-start-here.md#4-pin-a-baseline-change-something-grade-it) |
| **verdict** | What `enola check` prints: PASS or FAIL, what the change introduced, and what it could not see. | [Reading a verdict](20-reading-a-verdict.md) |
| **law** | A rule you declare about parts of your code, with a reason and a mode. Written in Ruby (`law`) or YAML (`rules:`), kept in `enola/constraints/`, and reported as `Constraint <id> violated`. Law, rule and constraint name the same thing. | [Writing laws](04-writing-laws.md) |
| **part** | A named set of files or facts a law speaks about: `part` in Ruby, an entry under `components:` in YAML, a role in a recipe. | [Writing laws](04-writing-laws.md#parts) |
| **mode** | How strictly a law holds: `advisory` reports and never fails, `ratchet` fails only new breaches, `strict` fails every breach. Start in ratchet. | [Writing laws](04-writing-laws.md#modes-dates-and-carve-outs) |
| **breach** | One place a law is broken, named by its witness: the edge or fact that breaks it. | [Writing laws](04-writing-laws.md) |
| **recipe** | A named bundle of laws over roles, such as `layered` or `rails-conventions`, which a repository binds to its own directories in one block (`use_recipe:`). enola ships some; [`recipes/`](../recipes/README.md) has more to copy. | [Writing laws](04-writing-laws.md#recipes) |
| **exemption** | A carve-out written on the law itself, naming one witness with an owner, a reason and a date. | [Writing laws](04-writing-laws.md#modes-dates-and-carve-outs) |
| **suppression** | A signed, temporary excuse in `.enola/suppressions.yaml`, the only override for a strict breach. | [Writing laws](04-writing-laws.md#modes-dates-and-carve-outs) |
| **partial verdict** | A grade over only the facts both snapshots share, because a provider or extractor ran on one side only. It names what it left out. | [Reading a verdict](20-reading-a-verdict.md#partial) |
| **declined** | `check` refused to grade (exit 3) because the two snapshots are not comparable. Not a pass. | [Reading a verdict](20-reading-a-verdict.md#declined) |
| **unevaluable** | A law the snapshot cannot answer, reported with its cause instead of a verdict. | [Writing laws](04-writing-laws.md#when-a-law-refuses) |
| **hook** | A command an agent runs at a fixed moment (a session starting, a turn ending). `enola install --hooks` writes enola's. | [Hooks and agents](06-hooks-and-agents.md) |
| **MCP** | Model Context Protocol, the way a coding agent calls a tool server. `enola` with no arguments is that server; its tools are `explore`, `impact_analysis` and the rest. | [Hooks and agents](06-hooks-and-agents.md#register-the-mcp-server) |
| **cluster** | Several repositories indexed as one graph, so a call from a client can be matched to the route it reaches. | [Beyond one repository](08-beyond-one-repo.md) |
| **seam** | A link between two repositories in a cluster: a client call matched to a route, a topic one publishes and another consumes. | [Beyond one repository](08-beyond-one-repo.md) |
| **intent page** | A Markdown page carrying an `enola_intent:` block, anchored to the code it governs. Optional; the knowledge-base track builds on it. | [A knowledge base](09-a-knowledge-base-with-enola.md) |

## Who makes what

- **enola** is by Dejan Menges, at
  [enola-labs/enola](https://github.com/enola-labs/enola). Its own
  documentation is the reference; these guides are a path through it.
- **These guides** are by Muhamed Isabegovic and are not part of
  enola-labs. Each release says which enola it was checked against: this
  one is enola-guides 0.9.0, checked against enola v0.4.35.
- **tabula**, **taha** and **cardo** are separate projects by the guides'
  author: tabula keeps a knowledge base of intent pages, taha runs agents
  on it, and cardo is a build derived from enola that tabula carries.
  None of them is public yet, so [guide 13](13-tabula.md) and
  [guide 14](14-taha.md) are a preview. Nothing else in these guides
  needs them.

## Next to the tools you already run

Linters, type checkers and tests judge the current tree against rules they
bring, file by file. Keep them; enola does not replace any of them.

Tools that check dependency rules (packwerk for Ruby packs, import-linter
for Python, dependency-cruiser for JavaScript, ArchUnit for the JVM) are
closer, and several keep a list of known violations so only new ones fail.
If one of them already enforces what you need in one language, keep it.
What enola adds is one graph across every language and repository in the
product; facts beyond imports (routes, tables, client calls, a runtime
capture); findings it computes without being given a rule (cycles, dead
code, query loops, hotspots); and the same graph handed to a coding agent
as tools, so it can ask what a change would touch before making it.

## Where next

[Start here](01-start-here.md): install, a snapshot, a graded change and a
first law, in ten minutes.

# Start here: the first useful answer in ten minutes

enola answers one question no linter can: **what did this change do to the
architecture?** It builds a graph of your code (modules, symbols, routes,
tables, and how they depend on each other), keeps that graph as a snapshot,
and grades a change by comparing the snapshot before it with the snapshot
after it. A dependency cycle that spans four files, a job that started
calling a controller, a table a second part began writing to: those are
invisible to tools that look at one file at a time, and they are what enola
reports. The words this guide uses (snapshot, baseline, law, verdict) are
defined in [what enola is](00-concepts.md).

This guide takes you from nothing to a graded change and a first law.
Everything here is checked against enola v0.4.35. Any newer release should
work; when you need the exact one, pin it as step 1 shows.

## 1. Install

No Go toolchain, no compiler, one binary:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/enola-labs/enola/main/install.sh | sh
enola --version
```

The script installs the newest release into `~/.local/bin` and fetches
the Rubydex library enola uses to resolve Ruby constants and ancestry
(more in [providers](07-providers.md)). The same binary is on PyPI as
`enola-cli` (`enola` was taken); install it as a tool, not into a
project's environment, and pin the version there when you need this
guide's exactly:

```bash
pipx install enola-cli==0.4.35      # or: uv tool install enola-cli==0.4.35
enola providers fetch rubydex       # once, after any install but the script
```

enola is not on npm. The npm package called `enola` is an unrelated tool
that deletes files; do not `npm install -g enola`. Every release,
with a checksum per platform, is on
[enola's releases page](https://github.com/enola-labs/enola/releases).

To try this guide somewhere safe first, the worked Python example is one
command away with [`enola-guides`](../README.md#these-guides-as-a-command):

```bash
enola-guides copy examples/python-service && cd python-service && git init -q
```

## 2. Look before you configure

One read-only command, nothing written:

```bash
enola --explain . 2>/dev/null
```

It prints what it found (languages, facts by kind, routes, tables,
dependencies), the architecture it detected (pattern, cycles, layer
violations), the coupling hotspots with their blast radius, and the code
health findings. Every command logs its progress on stderr, about a
hundred `[engine]` lines on a first run; `2>/dev/null` hides them. Nothing
here is a setting: enola detects every language in the tree and indexes
all of them into one graph, and the line `no mcp-arch.yaml ... using
built-in defaults` means exactly that. `--explain` does not grade your
laws; their breaches show in `enola check`, below.

## 3. Take the first snapshot

```bash
enola --generate .
```

This writes `.enola/` in the repository: the facts, the findings the
explainers computed, and a receipt saying which extractors and providers
ran and what they skipped. Read the receipt's census when something looks
missing: a file enola did not parse is named there, never silently
dropped. enola also records each snapshot in a history under `~/.enola/`,
which `enola gc` reports on and trims.

Ignore `.enola/` in git, all but one file you may add later, the
suppression ledger (see [writing laws](04-writing-laws.md#modes-dates-and-carve-outs)):

```gitignore
.enola/*
!.enola/suppressions.yaml
```

## 4. Pin a baseline, change something, grade it

```bash
enola baseline pin .
# ... edit code ...
enola check .
```

`check` takes a fresh snapshot of the working tree, compares it with the
pinned one, and prints what the change did: findings introduced, findings
resolved, edges added. It exits 0 unless you tell it what fails the
build:

```bash
enola check -fail-on constraints,cycles,layers .
```

`PASS` or `FAIL` leads the output. Three other words need reading before
you trust it, and the output names each. **DECLINED** (exit 3) means the
two snapshots are not comparable (a different enola version, changed
ignore globs, another repository), so re-pin the baseline rather than
reading it as a pass. A **partial verdict** (`PASS (partial verdict)` or
`FAIL (partial verdict)`) means a provider or extractor ran on one side
only: enola grades the facts both sides share and names what it left
ungraded. **unevaluable** on a law means the snapshot could not answer it,
named with its cause. [Reading a verdict](20-reading-a-verdict.md) has
every section of the output and every exit code.

## 5. Tell your agents

An agent uses enola through its MCP server, which is the `enola` binary
run with no arguments. Register it once; for Claude Code 2.1.287 or later,
with its tools loaded when the session starts:

```bash
claude mcp add-json enola '{"command":"enola","alwaysLoad":true}'
```

[Hooks and agents](06-hooks-and-agents.md#register-the-mcp-server) has the
line for Cursor, Codex, Copilot, opencode and Pi. Then the instructions
and the hooks:

```bash
enola install --hooks --targets claude --dry-run    # what it would write
enola install --hooks --targets claude
```

`install` writes enola's instructions into the files your coding agents
already read (`.claude/rules/enola.md` for Claude Code) and, with
`--hooks`, a session-start hook that pins the architecture as the
session's baseline and a stop hook that grades what the session changed.
Without `--targets` it writes for every agent it knows (Claude Code,
Cursor, Codex, Copilot, Pi, opencode), previews every change, and asks
before writing; `--yes` skips the question where there is no terminal.
`enola uninstall` reverses it byte for byte.

Restart the agent session, then:

```bash
enola doctor
```

reports whether the hooks actually fired, what they concluded, and whether
the pinned baseline can still be graded against. Until a session has
started in the repository it says `NEITHER HOOK HAS EVER RUN`; that is
the expected answer before the restart, and the one to worry about after
it. The hooks are written with the absolute path of your `enola`, so
before committing `.claude/settings.json` read
[what to commit](06-hooks-and-agents.md#what-to-commit).

## 6. Declare your first law

A law is a sentence about two parts of your code, its reason, and how
strictly it holds. Write it in YAML in `enola/constraints/`; YAML is the
form every team can write, whatever the language:

```yaml
# enola/constraints/domain.yaml
components:
  - name: domain
    match: ["shop/domain/**"]
  - name: api
    match: ["shop/api/**"]
rules:
  - id: the-domain-never-imports-the-api
    forbid: domain
    to: api
    via: imports
    mode: ratchet
    because: "the API calls the domain, never the other way round"
```

Change the globs to two directories of yours. Then:

```bash
enola constraints lint .     # is it valid, and what did each part match?
enola check .
```

`lint` prints each part with the members it matched (`domain  5
member(s)`); a part that matched nothing is the first thing to fix. A law
added by the change you are grading is reported apart from what the
change did, with what already breaks it:

```text
Newly declared (1) — a rule this change declares, re-forms or un-exempts
reports these on code the change did not touch. The baseline the rule starts
from, not regressions the change made:
```

Commit the law and pin again (`enola baseline pin .`). From now on a
change that adds a breach fails:

```text
$ enola check -fail-on constraints .
FAIL — 1 structural regression introduced.
…
Regressions (fail):
  - [constraints] 1.00 — Constraint the-domain-never-imports-the-api violated: module-edge: shop/domain -> shop/api -> shop/api via imports
```

`ratchet` reports what already breaks the law and fails only what a
change adds, which is the mode to start every law in. A breach is the
edge between two modules, so a second import along an edge that already
breaks the law is not a new breach.

**A shortcut, and when it applies.** `enola constraints init .`, after
a snapshot, writes a declaration binding every shipped recipe all of whose
roles it finds a directory for. Those are mostly Rails directories, so a
Rails application with controllers, models, jobs, mailers, policies,
serializers and view components gets `rails-conventions` and its
neighbours; most other trees get `nothing to bind`, with the directories
each recipe missed, and nothing is written (`--dry-run` prints the same
without writing, `--recipe NAME` binds one). Bind a recipe to your own
directories as [the Python guide](15-python.md) does, or write the law
yourself as above.

A Ruby team can write its laws in Ruby, parsed and never run:

```ruby
# enola/constraints/jobs.rb
Enola.architecture "shop" do
  rails   # declares controllers, models, jobs and the other Rails parts

  law "background jobs never invoke controller code" do
    jobs.must_not_call controllers
    why "rendering from a job goes through ApplicationController.renderer"
    mode :ratchet
  end
end
```

In a repository with no Ruby, that `.rb` file is itself the first Ruby
the snapshot sees, and a baseline pinned before it has none; the next
`check` is partial and grades a breach the law already had as new. Write
YAML there. Pinning again right after adding the file also clears it, but
folds the law's existing breaches into the baseline without listing them,
so read them first with `enola --generate . && enola constraints ledger .`.

[Writing laws](04-writing-laws.md) has the whole vocabulary, and
[`examples/laws`](../examples/laws/README.md) has twenty-six to copy.

## Where next

- Your stack: [Rails](02-rails.md), [Ember](03-ember.md),
  [Python](15-python.md), [TypeScript](16-typescript.md), [Go](17-go.md),
  [Rust](18-rust.md).
- [Constraints in CI](05-constraints-in-ci.md): the check on every pull
  request, with a template you copy.
- [Rolling out](19-rolling-out.md): adopting it on a repository that
  already has years of history, without failing everything on day one.
- [Hooks and agents](06-hooks-and-agents.md): what an agent does
  differently with enola connected.

# A Rails application

What enola sees in a Rails app, what the two Ruby providers add, and how
to go from the first snapshot to laws the team wrote. The worked example
is [`examples/rails-shop`](../examples/rails-shop): thirteen laws in the
Ruby DSL, one file each, with both providers configured.

## What the snapshot holds

From the Ruby extractor alone:

- **Symbols** for every class, module and method, with their calls,
  constant references and one-level superclass.
- **Routes** from `config/routes.rb` and every engine's route file,
  `resources` expanded, each route carrying its method and path and a
  `handled_by` edge to the controller action that serves it.
- **Storage** facts for every `ApplicationRecord` descendant: the model,
  its table (declared or derived), its columns and foreign keys when the
  schema is present.
- **Associations** with their macro, target and whether the target was
  declared (`class_name:`) or derived from the name.
- **Module edges** between directories, weighted by the symbol edges
  behind them, which is what cycle detection reads.

Run `enola --explain .` and then `enola --generate .`; the receipt in
`.enola/receipt.json` lists what each extractor parsed and skipped.

## The two providers

The Ruby extractor reads one file at a time, so it cannot tell which
class a constant names once nesting and inheritance are involved, or what
a class inherits through its mixins. Two providers settle that at snapshot
time, beside enola's own extraction. Both are built into the binary and
run against the Rubydex library, with no Ruby on the machine:

- **Rubydex** resolves constants through nesting and inheritance, types the
  receiver of a call, and linearises every class's ancestry with mixins in
  order. It reads your bundle's gem paths when `bundle` is on PATH so
  `ApplicationRecord` and `ViewComponent::Base` resolve.
- **Prism** adds the call edges a lexical walk can see: a call on the
  enclosing class, and `new` on a written constant. Named with no
  `command`, it reads the index Rubydex built in the same run.

```yaml
providers:
  - name: rubydex
  - name: prism
```

The install script and `enola upgrade` fetch the library the binary pins;
after `pip install enola-cli`, `go install` or a source build, run
`enola providers fetch rubydex` once. Leave `expected_version` off a
built-in: the binary already pins the library, and a pin that disagrees
with it skips the provider.

The configuration lives in `mcp-arch.yaml` at the repository root, the
one file name enola reads without being told. Rubydex indexes a tree that
has a `Gemfile`. With both providers a law can say "every class under
`ApplicationRecord`" and mean the resolved chain, not the text after `<`.
The [providers guide](07-providers.md) covers the census, the named skips,
the Prism script for a Ruby of your own, and the runtime capture.

## Name the parts

`enola constraints init .` writes `enola/constraints/recipes.yaml` binding
every shipped recipe all of whose roles your tree has a directory for. For
`rails-conventions` that means `app/controllers`, `app/jobs`, `app/models`,
`app/mailers`, `app/policies`, `app/serializers` and `app/components`; an
app missing one gets the recipe named with the directories it lacked and
not bound, so write the binding yourself and leave the missing role out:

```yaml
use_recipe:
  - recipe: rails-conventions
    as: rails
    mode: ratchet
    bind:
      controllers: { match: ["app/controllers/**"] }
      jobs: { match: ["app/jobs/**"] }
      models: { match: ["app/models/**"] }
      mailers: { match: ["app/mailers/**"] }
      policies: { match: ["app/policies/**"] }
      serializers: { match: ["app/serializers/**"] }
      view-components: { match: ["app/components/**"] }
```

Two roles are optional and off until you bind them: `helpers` and
`services`. Binding them brings three more laws (services and models
never reach helpers; the controller's request API stays out of models and
services). `rails-strict` is the same set with the concerns law added and
nothing advisory. `vanilla-rails` is for an app that keeps Rails plain and
wants its extra directories to stay empty with a stated reason each.

Two more recipes ship with enola and suit any Ruby tree. `ruby-conventions`
forbids the `get_`, `set_` and `is_` prefixes other languages bring along;
`supply-chain` forbids an unpinned dependency (see
[writing laws](04-writing-laws.md#laws-over-dependencies)).

`enola constraints lint .` shows every part with what it resolved to and
every rule a binding left unexpanded, which is how you check the tree
before the first verdict.

## The laws a Rails team writes

The recipe's laws, each with the reason it carries:

- jobs do not reach controllers (advisory, because the sanctioned path
  through `ApplicationController.renderer` reads as a crossing);
- models do not reach controllers;
- policies only answer, never enqueue;
- mailers do not enqueue;
- serializers do not reach controllers;
- view components do not enqueue and do not reach controllers;
- maintenance tasks do not reach controllers;
- with `helpers` bound: services and models never reach helpers;
- with `services` bound: the request API (`params`, `session`, `render`,
  `redirect_to`, `cookies`, `flash`) stays in controllers, stated as
  receiver-less calls so `request.params` on a typed receiver is not a
  breach.

Write your own beside them in Ruby, in any file under `enola/constraints/`:

```ruby
Enola.architecture "shop" do
  rails
  part :billing, files: ["app/billing/**", "app/models/invoice.rb"]
  part :orders, files: ["app/orders/**", "app/models/order.rb"],
                public: ["app/orders/public/**"]

  law "billing keeps to its own tables" do
    billing.storage_must_stay_home
    why "a part that writes another part's table owns a bug it cannot see"
    mode :ratchet
  end

  law "a mutating action is authorized" do
    part :mutating_actions, files: "app/controllers/**",
                            handles: [:post, :put, :patch, :delete]
    mutating_actions.must_reach :policies
    why "every write passes a policy before it touches a record"
    mode :ratchet
  end
end
```

The first law reads the storage facts: a member of `billing` reaching
`Order` is a breach that names the table `orders`, and the suggested cut
names the `orders` part's public member that already uses the model. The
second selects the code behind POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE routes through
the `handled_by` edges and demands a call into the policies, so the law
follows the routes rather than a list of actions.

## Packwerk

A repository that splits into packwerk packages gets the `packwerk`
explainer once enola finds the packages. It reads `package_paths` from
`packwerk.yml` and, when the file sets none, looks only at the root and
`packages/*`, where packwerk itself searches every directory; with packs
under `packs/` or `components/`, name them:

```yaml
# packwerk.yml
package_paths:
  - packs/*
```

The snapshot log says how many packages it found. The explainer compares
each `package.yml`'s declared
dependencies with what the package's code references, and reports both
sides. An undeclared reference names its file and line at confidence 0.9,
because a Ruby constant reaches its package by name; one already in
`package_todo.yml` is counted, not reported. A declared dependency the code
never references is reported at 0.7, since a constant reached through
`constantize`, a YAML class name or only a spec draws no edge. Gate on it
with `enola check -fail-on packwerk -min-confidence 0.9` once the todo
files say what you mean.

## Read a verdict

```bash
enola baseline pin .
# change something
enola check .
```

A constraint breach names the rule, the member, the edge and the reason,
leads its suggested actions with the smallest change the graph can see,
and says whether it is a decided-rule breach (exact membership over a
measured edge) or an advisory. `enola constraints explain app/jobs/x.rb`
answers what a file is a member of, by which selector, and which edges it
makes, which is the question to ask before arguing with a verdict.

## When the answer is "cannot evaluate"

A law over resolved ancestry without the Rubydex provider, a budget
without a runtime capture, a law across repositories in a one-repository
snapshot: each is reported as unevaluable with its cause and emits no
verdict. That is the design. A law nobody could measure must not read as
kept.

## Where next

- [`examples/laws`](../examples/laws/README.md): the Rails laws among the
  twenty-six (`rails-request-boundaries`, `rails-mutations-are-authorized`,
  `rails-strict-arrangement`, `foreign-keys`, `one-door`), each ready to
  copy.
- [Writing laws](04-writing-laws.md): every sentence, the modes, and the
  carve-outs.
- [Providers](07-providers.md): the census, the runtime capture, and a
  Prism script for a Ruby of your own.
- [Constraints in CI](05-constraints-in-ci.md): the check on every pull
  request.

# An Ember application

The same loop for the front end: what enola measures in an Ember app, and
how the conventions a team already writes in its style guide become laws.

## What the snapshot holds

The TypeScript and Ember extractors read `.ts`, `.js`, `.gts` and `.gjs`
and record, per class member, the things a convention talks about:

- the **decorators** a member carries (`action`, `cached`, `tracked`, `task`),
- the **fields it writes** (`args`, its own state, or any field at all),
- whether a member **takes parameters**,
- the **module a base class was imported from** (`@ember/controller` rather
  than the bare identifier `Controller`, which Stimulus also uses),
- the **kind** of each member (getter, constructor, method),
- **imports** by module path, including subpath imports from packages,
- and for test files, the calls a test makes, as `test_ref` facts a
  component can name by kind.

That is why the conventions below are laws and not lint rules: a component
is selected by what its facts carry, and a rule is set membership over
measured edges.

## The conventions, as a recipe

[`recipes/ember-conventions.yaml`](../recipes/ember-conventions.yaml) in
this repository carries nine conventions an Ember team recognises, with
the reason for each: no `@action` decorator, no framework controllers, no
render-modifier imports, constructors do not fetch, component tests carry
no fixtures, no legacy property accessor, arguments are not mutated, a
modifier takes its element, derivations do not write. Every role carries
its selector as a default, so the binding is short. Copy the recipe into
your repository with [`enola-guides`](../README.md#these-guides-as-a-command),
or download the file from this repository, and bind it:

```bash
enola-guides copy recipes/ember-conventions   # writes enola/recipes/ember-conventions.yaml
```

```yaml
# enola/constraints/ember.yaml
use_recipe:
  - recipe: ember-conventions
    as: app
    mode: ratchet
```

Two roles are optional and yours to name, because their far end is a
helper of your own: `task-factories` (the functions that build tracked
tasks in your app) and `fixture-setup` (the entry points of your fixture
library). Until you bind them the two laws that need them are left
unexpanded, and `enola constraints lint .` says so:

```yaml
    bind:
      task-factories: { match: ["app/utils/**"], name_pattern: "*.trackedFunction" }
      fixture-setup: { match: ["tests/helpers/**"] }
```

Copying the recipe, rather than pointing at a packaged copy, is the point:
the team reads the reasons, deletes a law it disagrees with, and reviews
the file on a pull request. A convention that appears from a tool is not
a convention.

## An Ember app inside a larger repository

When the app lives under a directory such as `frontend/`, override the
path-rooted roles key by key; the roles selected by a decorator or a
written field need nothing:

```yaml
use_recipe:
  - recipe: ember-conventions
    as: app
    mode: ratchet
    bind:
      components: { match: ["frontend/app/components/**"] }
      integration-tests: { match: ["frontend/tests/integration/**"] }
      constructors: { match: ["frontend/app/**"], name_pattern: "*.constructor" }
      fetchers: { match: ["frontend/app/services/**"] }
      legacy-accessor: { match: ["frontend/app/utils/**"], name_pattern: "*.get" }
      element-modifiers: { kind: symbol, match: ["frontend/app/components/**", "frontend/app/modifiers/**"] }
```

Or keep a house recipe in `enola/recipes/` with your paths as the
defaults, which is what a team with several conventions of its own ends
up doing anyway. A repository's recipe replaces a shipped one of the same
name, and lint notes it.

## Conventions the recipe cannot carry for you

Some laws hinge on a helper only your app has: a getter that unwraps a
promise through your helper must carry `@cached`, a reader of an async
relationship must pass it through your resolving helper. Write those in
your own recipe or inline, with your names:

```yaml
components:
  - name: promise-getters
    kind: symbol
    match: ["app/**"]
    where: { symbol_kind: getter }
rules:
  - id: promise-getters-are-cached
    require: promise-getters
    when_edge_to: ["*.unwrapPromise"]
    via: calls
    must_prop_contain: { prop: decorators, value: cached }
    mode: ratchet
    because: "A getter that unwraps a promise recomputes on every read unless it memoizes, and the renderer re-renders on each new value."
```

And a guide rule for what no fact can decide, delivered where the edit
happens:

```yaml
  - id: reach-for-an-existing-helper
    guide: components
    message: "Before writing a helper here, look in app/helpers and app/utils first."
    mode: notify
    because: "Duplication is a judgement about what two implementations mean, which no fact answers."
```

## What a breach looks like

`no-action-decorator violated: Dashboard.toggle is measured in actions`,
with the file and line, the reason from the recipe, and the suggested
action. A pull request that adds four breaches and fixes none reports
four findings; the 1,700 the codebase already carries stay out of the
way under `ratchet` and stop growing.

## Where next

- [`examples/ember-app`](../examples/ember-app): an Ember application
  bound to this recipe in one block.
- [Writing laws](04-writing-laws.md): every sentence and mode, and the
  carve-outs for a convention with one sanctioned exception.
- [Constraints in CI](05-constraints-in-ci.md): the check on every pull
  request.
- [Beyond one repository](08-beyond-one-repo.md): the app and the backend
  it calls as one graph, each client call matched to its route.

# Writing laws

A law is a sentence about parts of your application, its reason, and how
strictly it holds. Laws live in `enola/constraints/`, in Ruby (`.rb`,
parsed and never executed) or in YAML, and compile to the same
declaration. This guide is the Ruby surface; every sentence names a rule
form the YAML also accepts, and enola's
[constraints reference](https://github.com/enola-labs/enola/blob/main/docs/CONSTRAINTS.md)
gives each form in YAML. [`examples/laws`](../examples/laws/README.md)
has twenty-six complete laws, one directory each, to copy.

Ruby or YAML is a choice of reading, not of power: both compile to the
same thing, a repository may hold both, and a `.rb` law needs no Ruby on
the machine. In a repository with no Ruby, though, the first `.rb` file is
the first Ruby the snapshot sees and makes the next verdict partial
([start here](01-start-here.md#6-declare-your-first-law) shows what that
does), so write YAML there.

## Parts

```ruby
Enola.architecture "shop" do
  rails
  part :billing, files: ["app/billing/**"], public: ["app/billing/public/**"]
  part :records, ancestor: "ApplicationRecord"
  part :getters, files: "app/**", kind: :symbol, where: { symbol_kind: "getter" }
  part :mutating_actions, files: "app/controllers/**", handles: [:post, :put, :patch, :delete]
  part :decided, governed_by: "docs/decisions/*.md"
  part :api, files: "config/**", kind: :route
  part :tables, files: "app/models/**", kind: :storage
end
```

`rails` declares the conventional parts (controllers, models, jobs,
mailers, policies, serializers, view components, helpers, services,
concerns) from the directories Rails keeps them in. A `part` takes
`files` (bounded globs), `kind` (symbol, module, route, storage,
dependency, and the reference kinds test_ref, file_ref, lint), `named` (one prefix, one
suffix or an exact name), `where` (a conjunction over measured props),
`owns: :methods` (a member's methods count as the member's when an edge
is walked), `ancestor` (every class under it, over resolved ancestry),
`public` (the files that are the part's surface), `handles` (the code a
route of those methods reaches), and `governed_by` (the files a knowledge
page anchors, with `status:` or `supersedes:` qualifiers). A part name
written in snake_case is the component `snake-case`.

Quote every value in a `where:` hash, booleans and numbers included:
`where: { pinned: "false" }`. In v0.4.35 the Ruby surface reads only
strings and symbols there and drops any other value without a word, so
`pinned: false` selects every package, pinned or not. `constraints lint`
shows each part's selector as it resolved (`where pinned=false`), which is
how to see that a condition arrived.

## Sentences

| Sentence | What it states |
|---|---|
| `a.must_not_call :b` | no `calls` edge from a into b (`via :imports` on its own line in the law for another edge kind) |
| `a.must_not_call "params", receiver: :none` | no receiver-less call to a literal |
| `a.must_not_reach :b` | no path from a to b over any edge kind |
| `a.may_only_call :b, :c` | a's edges land only in b and c |
| `a.is_reached_only_by :b` | only b reaches a |
| `a.stays_inside except: :b` | a's non-public members are reached only from inside a, or from b |
| `a.must_reach :b` / `a.must_be_reached_by :b` | an edge exists, outbound or inbound |
| `a.must_follow :b, :c` | a's members that reach b also reach c |
| `a.must_define :call` / `a.must_define_one_of :call, :run` | every class member defines the method, or one of them |
| `a.names_must_match "*Job"` / `a.names_must_match "with_*", requires: "without_*"` | a naming convention, or a pair |
| `a.names_must_not_match "get_*"` | a forbidden prefix, suffix or name |
| `a.must_be_empty` | the part matches nothing |
| `a.at_most 12` | a cap on the membership (`growth 2` lets it exceed the baseline's count by two) |
| `a.must_carry prop: "decorators", value: "cached"` | every member carries a prop (narrow with `when_calling` or `when_carrying`) |
| `a.must_not_cycle_with :b, :c` | no dependency cycle among the parts |
| `a.must_not_reach_includers` | a mixin never reaches a class that includes it |
| `a.storage_must_stay_home` | every table a member reaches is the part's own |
| `a.must_keep_budget metric: :queries, max: 20` | no frame in a exceeds the budget a runtime capture measured |
| `a.must_have_consumer` | every route in a has a client somewhere in the cluster |
| `a.must_be_unique_across by: :table` | no table is owned by two repositories |
| `a.must_be_governed` | every file in a is anchored by a knowledge page |
| `a.advises "look in app/utils first"` | guidance delivered where the edit happens, never a verdict |

`via` is a word of the law, not of the sentence: write `via :imports` on
its own line inside `law ... do`. In v0.4.35 a `via:` keyword written on
the sentence (`a.must_not_call b, via: :imports`) is dropped without a
word and the law reads `calls`; the breach's witness ends in `via calls`
or `via imports`, which is how to see which one arrived.

A breach is named by its witness, the edge or fact that breaks the law.
An edge law's witness is the edge between two modules
(`module-edge: shop/domain -> shop/api -> shop/api via imports`), so a second import
along an edge that already breaks the law is the same breach, not a new
one, and a ratchet law does not fail it.

## Modes, dates and carve-outs

Every law carries `why` (`because:` in YAML): the reason is what a reader
of a breach needs to judge it. `mode` decides how strictly it holds:

| Mode | A breach is reported as | What fails `check` |
|---|---|---|
| `ratchet` (the default) | `Constraint <id> violated`, confidence 1.00 | only a breach the change added |
| `advisory` | `Advisory constraint <id> violated`, confidence 0.90 | nothing, under the default confidence floor of 1.00 |
| `strict` | `Strict constraint <id> violated` | every breach, including those the baseline already had, even with no `-fail-on` |

Start every law in ratchet. A law that fails only what a change adds can
be adopted on a repository that breaks it in a hundred places; strict is
for a law decided to hold now, after the backlog is gone. Advisory stays
silent in the gate only while the gate's confidence floor is above 0.90:
`-min-confidence 0.8` lets an advisory breach fail the build.
[Constraints in CI](05-constraints-in-ci.md) says how the template sets
the floor.

`since "2026-08-01"` dates a law against the architecture history: a
breach the revision at that date already carried is reported, one
introduced after it is graded.

- Where the history holds no revision that old, git dates the breach
  instead, by the author date of the line that witnesses it (cached in
  `.enola/blame_cache.json`).
- A breach git cannot date (no git, an uncommitted line, a shallow clone
  whose boundary is newer than the date) grades as if the law had no
  date, and the run says so once. A CI checkout that runs dated laws
  fetches enough history.

When a breach should not fail the build, there are four answers, and the
earliest one that is true is the right one:

1. **Fix it.** The code is wrong and the law stands.
2. **Exempt it.** The witness is decided to be outside the law, for good
   and with a reason. The exemption is written on the law, names the
   exact witness string the breach is titled with, and carries an owner,
   a reason and a date:

   ```ruby
   law "controllers reach the schema through one door" do
     controllers.must_not_call schema
     why "a second door is a second place to forget authentication"
     exempt "Api::GraphqlController#execute -> AppSchema.execute via calls",
            because: "the one sanctioned entry point", owner: "platform", since: "2026-08-22"
   end
   ```

   ```yaml
   exempt:
     - witness: "Api::GraphqlController#execute -> AppSchema.execute via calls"
       owner: platform
       because: "the one sanctioned entry point"
       since: "2026-08-22"
   ```

   An exempted witness is reported in its own `Exempted by declaration`
   section on every run and never fails. An exemption that matches
   nothing is itself a finding: the breach is gone, or the witness was
   mistyped. [`examples/laws/one-door`](../examples/laws/one-door) carries
   one.
3. **Suppress it.** The breach is real, but a strict law must not block
   while it is worked off. A suppression is a signed, temporary entry in
   `.enola/suppressions.yaml`, committed (keep it out of `.gitignore`)
   and never written by enola:

   ```yaml
   entries:
     - rule: company-fk             # or finding_title_prefix: "…"; exactly one
       owner: alice
       reason: "legacy tables migrate in Q4"
       date: "2026-08-10"
   ```

   A suppressed breach is reported under `Suppressed` and never fails;
   an invalid file is rejected whole.
4. **Leave it in the baseline.** A ratchet law already ignores a breach
   the baseline had. Nobody decided anything; that is the reason to use
   one of the forms above for anything somebody did decide.

`enola constraints ledger .` (below) shows, per law, how much is excused
by each of these and by whom.

## Recipes

A recipe is a named bundle of laws over roles, bound to your directories
in one block. enola ships `layered`, `clean`, `ports-and-adapters`,
`cqrs`, `event-driven`, `modular-monolith`, `rails-conventions`,
`rails-strict`, `vanilla-rails`, `ruby-conventions` and `supply-chain`;
[`recipes/`](../recipes/README.md) has more to copy into your own
`enola/recipes/`.

```yaml
# enola/constraints/layers.yaml
use_recipe:
  - recipe: layered
    as: shop
    mode: ratchet
    bind:
      presentation: { match: ["shop/api/**"] }
      application: { match: ["shop/services/**"] }
      domain: { match: ["shop/domain/**"] }
      infrastructure: { match: ["shop/repositories/**"] }
```

Each rule the recipe expands is reported under the binding's name
(`shop/presentation-reaches-application-only`), and `constraints lint`
says how many rules each binding expanded. `layered`, `clean` and
`ports-and-adapters` are alternative arrangements: bind the one your code
follows. `enola constraints init` binds every recipe whose roles it
finds, so on a large Rails application it can bind several at once, and
`rails-conventions` beside `rails-strict` states some laws twice, in two
modes; `init --recipe NAME` binds one.

A recipe's rules name one edge kind each, and `via:` matches that kind
exactly. `layered`'s two domain rules
(`domain-knows-no-infrastructure`, `domain-knows-no-presentation`) read
`depends_on`, which the Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust extractors do not
write; they write `imports`. On those trees the two rules are silent
whatever the domain imports, and the language guides state the domain's
law over `imports` beside the recipe. The three rules over `calls` hold
as written.

## Laws over dependencies

Every direct dependency a manifest declares (`Gemfile`, `package.json`,
`go.mod`, `Cargo.toml`, `pyproject.toml`, `requirements.txt`,
`pubspec.yaml`) is a `kind: dependency` fact named by its Package URL
(`pkg:gem/rails`), carrying the constraint as written, the version the
lockfile resolved and `pinned`. `pinned` is absent, not false, when a
lockfile sits beside the manifest that enola cannot read, so a law over it
stays silent rather than wrong. The shipped `supply-chain` recipe is the
law that every dependency is pinned:

```yaml
use_recipe:
  - recipe: supply-chain
    as: supply
    bind:
      unpinned-dependencies: {}
```

or the same in Ruby:

```ruby
part :unpinned, kind: :dependency, where: { type: "package", pinned: "false" }

law "dependencies are pinned" do
  unpinned.must_be_empty
  why "a range is a different program on every build"
  mode :ratchet
end
```

A repository with no manifest enola reads gets a finding that the
selector cannot be evaluated, never a silent pass. What a repository means
to depend on, with a purpose for each, goes under `dependencies:` in its
`enola-intent.yaml`, and the intent check reports the difference between
that list and what the manifests declare.

## Reading what a law did

```bash
enola constraints lint .
enola constraints explain app/billing/charge.rb
enola check .
```

`lint` validates every declaration and shows what each part resolved to;
`explain` answers, for one file, which parts admit it, by which selector,
and which edges it makes; `check` grades the working tree against the
pinned baseline (`enola baseline pin .` first, or it exits 2 with `no
pinned baseline`). A law added since the baseline is listed under `Newly
declared` with every breach it already has; that list is how to see what
a new law will say before it can fail anything. A breach leads its
suggested actions with the smallest cut the graph can see: the far
part's public member with the same name, its public surface, the part
the offender's other edges mostly reach, the lightest edge of a cycle,
the owner's member that already reaches a table. When the facts support
no cut, the action says so.

## When a law refuses

A law that the snapshot cannot answer is reported as unevaluable with its
cause and emits no verdict: `no_resolved_ancestry` (no Rubydex provider
ran), `no_runtime_capture` (no capture for a budget), `no_counterparty`
(one repository where the law needs two), `no_frame_in_members` (a
capture whose frames all lie outside the part, as a capture keyed by spec
files does), `no_compiled_pages` (no knowledge pages in the snapshot), `unmeasured_property` (a `where` over a
prop no extractor emits, with the nearest measured names suggested). Fix
the snapshot, not the law.

## How much of the law is excused

```bash
enola constraints ledger .
```

reports each law's breaches beside the ones its exemptions and
suppressions excuse, each excuse with its owner, reason and age, and
names the excuses that now match nothing. A law that holds only because
everything is exempt shows as exactly that. `--json` writes the same as
one document.

## Mining laws you already keep

```bash
enola constraints mine .
```

proposes candidate laws from what the snapshot shows holds today (a
namespace every task already lives in, a prefix every public tool already
carries), each with the count it was mined at, so a team can adopt what
it practises before it writes what it wants.

## Where next

- [Constraints in CI](05-constraints-in-ci.md): the laws graded on every
  pull request.
- [Rolling out](19-rolling-out.md): which laws to start with on a
  repository that already breaks them, and when to enforce.
- [Reading a verdict](20-reading-a-verdict.md): every section a breach can
  land in.

# Constraints in CI

The check that grades every pull request against its base branch, reports
what the change added, and never fails the build until the team decides it
should. On GitHub that is one step, [enola-action](#on-github-enola-action);
on any other CI, or where you want the comment grouped per rule,
[`templates/enola-check.sh`](../templates/enola-check.sh) is the script and
most of this guide is why it looks the way it does.

## On GitHub: enola-action

```yaml
# .github/workflows/architecture.yml
on: pull_request
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  architecture:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: enola-labs/enola-action@v2
        with:
          version: 0.4.35
          fail-on: constraints
          warn-only: true
```

It resolves the pull request's exact base commit, generates both sides on
the runner, annotates the lines that introduced a finding, and writes the
delta to the job summary. `version` pins the release; left out, it is
`latest`, and a check that passed yesterday can fail today with no change
of yours. `pr-comment: true` also posts the report as one comment edited
in place (it needs `pull-requests: write`), and `sarif: true` writes a
SARIF 2.1.0 file for code scanning, exposed as the `sarif-file` output.
Its `status` output is one of `clean`, `partial_clean`, `regression`,
`partial_regression`, `usage_error` and `incomparable`, and `partial`
says whether the verdict graded only the producers both sides share.

The action downloads enola but not the Rubydex library. A repository with
Ruby installs both, pinned, and hands the action that binary; without it
the Ruby is graded without its providers on both sides alike, so the
verdict looks whole and quietly misses everything Rubydex resolves:

```yaml
      - name: Install enola 0.4.35 and the Rubydex library it pins
        run: |
          v=0.4.35; a=enola-$v-linux-amd64
          curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/enola-labs/enola/releases/download/v$v/$a.tar.gz"
          curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/enola-labs/enola/releases/download/v$v/$a.sha256"
          sha256sum -c "$a.sha256"
          tar -xzf "$a.tar.gz"
          mkdir -p "$RUNNER_TEMP/enola" && mv "$a" "$RUNNER_TEMP/enola/enola"
          "$RUNNER_TEMP/enola/enola" providers fetch rubydex
      - uses: enola-labs/enola-action@v2
        with:
          binary: ${{ runner.temp }}/enola/enola
          fail-on: constraints
          warn-only: true
```

Removing `warn-only` is the team's decision, made once the reports have
been read for a while; [rolling out](19-rolling-out.md) says when.

## Any other CI: the template

[`templates/enola-check.sh`](../templates/enola-check.sh) and its renderer
[`templates/enola-findings.rb`](../templates/enola-findings.rb) are the
same check as a script. `enola-guides copy templates/enola-check` writes
both to `ci/`, side by side; run `ci/enola-check.sh` as a CI step.

What it needs from the CI:

- **The full history** of the base branch and the change: on GitHub
  `fetch-depth: 0`, on GitLab `GIT_DEPTH: 0`. A shallow clone has no
  merge-base, and on CI the script fails the step saying so rather than
  skipping.
- **A clean working tree**, since it checks out the merge-base to snapshot
  it.
- `curl`, `tar` and `sha256sum`. Optional: `ruby`, to group the comment
  per rule (without it the comment is enola's own `check --summary`), and
  `gh`, to post the comment (without it the comment is printed).

And what it reads:

| Variable | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `ENOLA_VERSION` | the first line of a committed `.enola-version`, else `0.4.35` | the release it downloads, checks against its checksum and caches |
| `ENOLA_CHECK_ENFORCE` | unset: report only | `1` makes it a gate that exits with `check`'s own code |
| `ENOLA_CHECK_WATCHED` | `constraints,query-loops,layers,cycles` | the explainers whose new findings it watches (`-fail-on`) |
| `ENOLA_CHECK_MIN_CONFIDENCE` | unset: enola's floor of 1.00 | lowers the floor; at 0.90 or below, advisory laws fail too |
| `PR_NUMBER` | unset | the pull request to read the base from and comment on |

## The shape

1. **Pin a release.** The script downloads one version of the binary,
   verifies its checksum, and caches it per version and platform. A
   floating version is how a check that passed yesterday fails today with
   no change of yours. A committed `.enola-version` pins it in one place.
2. **Grade against the pull request's base, not against main.** A stacked
   pull request whose parent declares new rules would otherwise report the
   parent's whole backlog as its own. Push-triggered builds often know the
   pull request number but not its base, so the script asks the forge for
   it and falls back to `main` only when there is no pull request at all.
3. **Two snapshots, one verdict.** Check out the merge-base, generate;
   check out the head, generate; `enola check -baseline previous`.
4. **Configure the providers the runner has.** In a tree with a `Gemfile`,
   the script fetches the Rubydex library the pinned binary names and
   configures the built-in `rubydex` and `prism` providers, which need no
   Ruby on the runner. A provider of your own (eslint, a runtime capture)
   is one more entry in the same block. Each absence is a named line in
   the log, never a silent drop, and the same configuration generates both
   snapshots and grades them, so they stay comparable.
5. **Watch a few explainers, report only, then enforce.** By default the
   step runs `check -fail-on constraints,query-loops,layers,cycles
   -warn-only`: it reports what those explainers added and exits 0.
   Setting `ENOLA_CHECK_ENFORCE=1` is the team's decision, made once the
   comments have been read for a while; [rolling out](19-rolling-out.md)
   says when. The floor stays at enola's 1.00, so an advisory law (0.90)
   and an estimate (an inferred layer, a query reached through an
   interface) are reported and never fail. A strict law fails on every
   breach, new or not.
6. **Render for a reader, grouped per rule.** The verdict's JSON becomes a
   comment with four sections in this order: **Watched** (the watched
   explainers' new findings at or above the floor, grouped per rule with a
   count and three examples, constraints first; under enforcement the
   headline is "This blocks the merge."), **Below the floor** (the watched
   explainers' findings under it, which never fail), **Declared** (rules
   this change declares, reported on code it did not touch, the baseline
   each rule starts from) and **Also noticed** (everything outside the
   watched set). One comment per pull request, found by a marker and
   edited in place; a clean run updates an existing comment and posts
   nothing new.

## Exit codes, and why "did not run" fails

| `check` exits | The step | The comment |
|---|---|---|
| 0, clean | passes | posted, or an existing one updated |
| 1, regression | passes while reporting only; fails under `ENOLA_CHECK_ENFORCE=1` | posted, naming what fails |
| 2, error (no baseline, a bad flag) | fails on CI as "did not run" | none |
| 3, declined (not comparable) | fails on CI as "did not run" | none |

On a laptop, 2 and 3 skip with the reason instead. Read "did not run" as
"not asked", and fix what made the pair incomparable: a different enola
version or different ignore globs on the two sides. It is never a pass.

When only the producers differ (a provider whose tool was missing on one
side, or a language or the first Markdown file appearing in the change),
`check` grades the facts both snapshots share and says the verdict is
partial; the comment names each producer it left out and the side that
lacked it, because a regression among those facts is not reported. The
script generates both snapshots with the same configuration, so a partial
verdict on CI means the change added a kind of file the base did not
have, or a tool the runner lacks, not a misconfigured step.

Under `-warn-only` the JSON verdict's `status` reads `clean` even when
regressions were reported, and enola-action's `status` output follows it;
read the findings, not `status`, to know whether anything was found while
the check only reports.

## Other shapes of the verdict

`check` writes the same verdict in several shapes, chosen with `-format`:
`text` (the default), `json` (what the template renders), `sarif` for code
scanning, `annotations` for the CI's line annotations (`-host github` or
`-host buildkite`, with `-link` naming the pull request's files view on
Buildkite), and `summary`, a plain-language account for a reader who does
not know the explainer names. `summary-json` is that account as JSON. Each
shape grades nothing of its own, so the exit code is the verdict's
whichever one printed it. [Reading a verdict](20-reading-a-verdict.md)
has every section.

`-reviewers` adds who owns the modules the change touched, read from git
authorship, and suggests a reviewer when the author is a minor
contributor; it never fails the run.

## Reproduce locally

```bash
bash ci/enola-check.sh     # or wherever you keep it
```

The script is written to run on a laptop: without the forge's credentials
it skips the comment and prints the verdict, and it leaves the checkout on
the branch it found.

## Adapting the template

The template targets a generic CI with three places you fill in, each
marked `FILL IN`: how the binary is fetched (a release asset URL and its
checksum), how the pull request's base branch is read (an environment
variable on pull-request builds, a forge API call on push builds), and how
the comment is posted (a small script against the forge's comments API).
Everything between, the two snapshots and the verdict and the rendering,
is the same on every CI.

## Where next

- [Rolling out](19-rolling-out.md): which laws to start with, and when to
  enforce.
- [Reading a verdict](20-reading-a-verdict.md): every section of the
  output.
