# Hooks and agents

enola is most useful when nobody has to remember to run it. An agent
gets three things: the MCP server, so it can ask the graph; the
instructions and hooks `enola install` writes, so it asks before
searching and is graded when it stops; and, optionally, a skill. This
guide sets up each and says what changes in the agent's work.

## What the agent does differently

| When | Without enola | With the server and `install --hooks` |
|---|---|---|
| The session starts | nothing | the architecture is pinned as the session's baseline, and the agent is told enola's tools are there |
| It needs to know what depends on X | greps for the name, and misses a caller reached through an interface or a package in between | asks `impact_analysis` or `explore`; in Claude Code its first two tree searches are refused with a pointer to the tool that answers |
| It is about to edit a file | reads the file | can ask `constraints_for` and `plan_check` which laws bind it and what the edit would breach |
| The turn ends | reports it is done | the stop hook grades the change and speaks only when it introduced a regression, a finding no policy enforces, or could not be compared |

## Register the MCP server

The server is the `enola` binary run with no arguments; the agent
starts it. Register it once per machine:

| Agent | Register with |
|---|---|
| Claude Code 2.1.287 or later | `claude mcp add-json enola '{"command":"enola","alwaysLoad":true}'` |
| an older Claude Code | `claude mcp add enola enola` |
| Codex | `codex mcp add enola -- enola` |
| Copilot in VS Code | `code --add-mcp '{"name":"enola","command":"enola"}'` |
| Cursor | `{ "mcpServers": { "enola": { "command": "enola" } } }` in `.cursor/mcp.json`, or `~/.cursor/mcp.json` for every project |
| opencode | nothing: `enola install --targets opencode` registers it in `.opencode/opencode.json` |
| Pi | nothing: Pi has no MCP client, so `enola install --targets pi` writes `.pi/extensions/enola.js`, which serves every tool as `enola_<tool>` |

`alwaysLoad` loads enola's tools when the session starts. Without it,
Claude Code lists them by name only (deferred) and the agent spends a turn
loading them through ToolSearch while a file search is already in reach;
the session-start hook tells it how, in one call. With a config file,
pass it in `args`
(`'{"command":"enola","args":["mcp-arch.yaml"],"alwaysLoad":true}'`).
After `enola upgrade`, restart the session so the server process is the
new binary.

## The hooks

```bash
enola install --hooks --targets claude --dry-run   # preview, write nothing
enola install --hooks --targets claude
```

writes enola's instructions into the file your agent already reads
(`.claude/rules/enola.md`, `.cursor/rules/enola.mdc`, `AGENTS.md`,
`.github/instructions/enola.instructions.md`, ...) and wires the hooks:

- **session start** pins the architecture as the session's baseline, the
  "before" every later grade compares against;
- **stop** grades what the session changed against that baseline when the
  agent finishes a turn, and speaks only when the change introduced a
  regression or a finding no policy enforces, or when it could not compare
  at all (then the remedy is to re-pin, not to doubt the change). It says
  each distinct report once per session.

In Claude Code two more: a `PreToolUse` hook refuses the session's first
two file searches over a tree (the `Grep` and `Glob` tools, or a `find`,
a recursive `grep` or an `rg` over a directory in the shell) with a
pointer to the enola tool that answers the question, and a `PostToolUse`
hook records that an enola tool was used, which ends the refusals. A
`grep` of files the agent names, or of piped output, is a read and goes
through; a search run again after a refusal goes through. With
`alwaysLoad` set, the refusals rarely fire.

`install` without `--targets` writes for every agent it knows (Claude
Code, Cursor, Codex, Copilot, Pi, opencode). It previews every change and
asks before writing (`--yes` where there is no terminal), never creates a
shared file such as `AGENTS.md` that was not already there, and
`enola uninstall` reverses it byte for byte. `--global` writes the
user-level files instead (`~/.claude/settings.json` and
`~/.claude/rules/enola.md` for Claude Code), for every repository you
open.

In a **folder of repositories** (a directory whose subfolders are git
repositories, such as a backend beside its clients), `--hooks` installs
only Claude Code's steering hooks: the session-start note, the search
refusal and the use recorder. A baseline needs one repository, so there
is no stop hook there; run `install --hooks` inside each repository whose
changes should be graded.

Two agents get more than instructions, because they lack what the others
have. **Pi** gets the extension above, with or without `--hooks`, since
without it Pi has no enola tools at all. **opencode** has no hook
configuration of this shape, so `--targets opencode` registers the server
in `.opencode/opencode.json` and, with `--hooks`, installs
`.opencode/plugin/enola.js`, which names the enola tool in the
descriptions of `grep`, `glob` and `list` and refuses a session's first
searches (`ENOLA_OPENCODE_GATE=off` keeps the rest and drops the
refusals).

### Did they fire?

Restart the agent session after installing, then:

```bash
enola doctor
```

reports whether the hooks actually fired in this repository (when each
last ran and what it concluded), whether the pinned baseline can still be
graded against, whether the Rubydex library is in place, and whether a
newer release is out. Before any session has started it says `NEITHER
HOOK HAS EVER RUN`; after a restart, that line means the agent is not
reading the configuration. A hook that is configured but never fires
looks exactly like one that fires and stays quiet, and `doctor` is the
only thing that tells them apart. Each hook has a 60-second timeout; on a
repository where a snapshot takes longer (see
[rolling out](19-rolling-out.md#1-measure-it-on-your-repository)), the stop hook can time
out.

### The Claude Code plugin

enola's repository is also a Claude Code plugin marketplace:

```text
/plugin marketplace add enola-labs/enola
/plugin install enola@enola
```

The plugin registers the MCP server, the session-start and stop hooks, and
two skills: one routing an architecture question to the tool that answers
it, and `/enola:setup`, which checks for the CLI and runs the install
script when it is missing. It configures and does not install, so `enola`
must be on PATH. It carries neither the search refusal nor the
tool-loading line `install --hooks` adds. Choose the plugin or
`install --hooks`, not both: both register the same hooks, and the
session would be pinned and graded twice.

## What to commit

`install` writes the absolute path of the `enola` that ran it into the
hook commands (`/home/you/.local/bin/enola hook stop`). Committed, that
path is wrong on every other machine, and a hook that cannot start never
breaks a session, so nobody notices. Commit what the team shares and let
each developer install the rest:

| Commit | Do not commit |
|---|---|
| `enola/constraints/`, `enola/recipes/` | `.enola/`, except `.enola/suppressions.yaml` |
| `mcp-arch.yaml`, `enola-intent.yaml` | the hook entries in `.claude/settings.json`, `.codex/hooks.json` |
| `.enola/suppressions.yaml` | |
| `.claude/rules/enola.md` and the other instruction files (they carry no paths) | |

Each developer then runs `enola install --hooks --global` once, which
puts the hooks in their own user settings with their own path, for every
repository they open.

## Turning it off

- One agent, or all: `enola uninstall` (`--targets` to choose, `--global`
  for the user-level files) reverses what `install` wrote.
- The search refusal alone: in opencode, `ENOLA_OPENCODE_GATE=off`; in
  Claude Code it has no switch, so register the server with `alwaysLoad`
  (it then rarely fires) or remove the `PreToolUse` entry.
- The update check: `ENOLA_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1`.
- The snapshot history under `~/.enola/`: `history: { enabled: false }`
  in `mcp-arch.yaml` stops recording it, and `enola gc` reports what it
  holds and trims it.

## The MCP tools an agent should reach for

| Before a change | |
|---|---|
| `explore` | what is in here and what touches it; the one to reach for first |
| `impact_analysis` | what transitively depends on this, before touching it |
| `endpoint_impact` | who calls this HTTP endpoint, and which screens sit behind the callers |
| `traverse`, `find_path`, `show_symbol`, `query_facts` | how something is wired, instead of reconstructing it from files; `find_path` takes sets (`from_nodes`, `to_nodes`) to ask how any of one group reaches any of another in one search, and `show_symbol` takes several names in one call |
| `governing_intent` | which decision pages govern this file or symbol, and which code a page governs |
| `constraints_for`, `plan_check` | which declared laws bind a path, and what a planned edit would breach before it exists |
| `set_baseline` | pin the architecture as it is, once, early |

| After a change | |
|---|---|
| `generate_snapshot`, `diff_snapshot` | what the change actually did: findings introduced or resolved, coupling added; `generate_snapshot` takes `repo_paths` to index several repositories as one graph |
| `query_insights` | the explainers' findings, rather than re-deriving them |
| `snapshot_receipt`, `compare_receipts` | what a graph was generated over and where its limits are, and whether two snapshots are comparable enough to trust a diff between them |
| `architecture_blame`, `architecture_history` | when a dependency entered the architecture, and how it changed over time |

| Looking for trouble | |
|---|---|
| `find_orphans` | what nothing references any more |
| `package_metrics` | how stable and how abstract a package is, and its distance from the main sequence |
| `analyze_performance` | where the cost grows with the input |
| `coverage_report` | which cross-repository edges resolved and which were missed |

## The same questions from a shell

A hook, a review bot or a person without an agent asks the graph through
the CLI. Each command reads the current snapshot, says when it was written
and whether it matches the working tree, and takes `--json`:

```bash
enola impact 'kind:symbol OrdersController' .   # what depends on it, by hop depth
enola endpoint 'GET /api/v2/orders' .           # the controller, models, tables and callers behind a route
enola plan --paths app/jobs/receipt_job.rb .    # the laws governing a path and its blast radius, before the edit
enola flows .                                   # the ways into the program, ranked by what each reaches
enola constraints ledger .                      # per law, the breaches reported beside the ones excused
enola dashboard --open .                        # the snapshot in a read-only local browser view
```

`plan --patch` evaluates the verdicts a diff would produce over a scratch
copy before it lands; `flows --through <symbol>` lists only the flows
that reach a symbol. Every flag takes one dash or two (`-paths` and
`--paths` are the same). `enola help <command>` prints any command's
page, and `--help` never runs the command it describes.

## The skill

[`templates/skills/enola/SKILL.md`](../templates/skills/enola/SKILL.md) is
the skill to drop into your agent's skills directory
(`enola-guides copy skills/enola`). It says when to use the graph (a
change whose impact is not obvious, a change to how modules depend on
each other, a hook or CI finding), which tool answers which question, and
how to read a finding: it names the structural change and the rule it
crossed, and a "could not compare" means the baseline is stale, not that
the change is wrong. `install` already writes most of that into the
agent's instructions (`.claude/rules/enola.md`); add the skill when you
want it loaded only for architecture work, rather than in every session.
Three more skills for any repository sit beside it: `enola-laws`,
`enola-grade-before-push` and `enola-intent-first`.

## Intent first, optionally

Teams that keep decision records can compile them into the graph: a page
carrying an `enola_intent:` block with anchors (repository and path)
becomes an intent fact, `governing_intent` answers which pages govern a
file, and the `governed_by` component key and `require_governed` form turn
that into laws (see [writing laws](04-writing-laws.md)). A pre-edit hook
that reads `governing_intent` for the file about to change and puts the
decision trail in front of the agent is
[the intent-first gate](10-hooks.md#the-intent-first-gate-pretooluse-on-edit-and-write);
the [knowledge-base track](09-a-knowledge-base-with-enola.md) builds the
rest. Nothing above needs it.

## Where next

- [Rolling out](19-rolling-out.md): the hooks, the CI check and the laws
  adopted on a team, and what each costs.
- [Knowledge-base hooks](10-hooks.md): the intent-first gate and the
  stop-time debt, for a team that keeps decision records.

# Providers

A provider contributes facts to the graph that no extractor measures: the
result of running another tool, a capture of the app at run time, a
language engine's resolution. enola runs the configured providers at
snapshot time, validates everything they emit against the fact schema,
refuses a provider's whole output on the first invalid line, and records
in the receipt what each provider contributed and what it skipped.

## Configure

```yaml
# mcp-arch.yaml
providers:
  - name: rubydex
  - name: prism
  - name: eslint
    command: ["node", "/path/to/enola_eslint_provider.mjs"]
    expected_version: "0.1.0"
```

enola runs an external provider twice: once with `--version`, to check
the pin, and once with the repository path. The provider prints its facts
as JSONL on stdout and one line on stderr saying what it read and what it
skipped, its census. A provider with no
`command` is one the binary carries itself: `rubydex` and `prism`. An
`expected_version` pins what the provider must answer, and a provider that
answers anything else is skipped by name; pin a script to its own
`PROVIDER_VERSION`, and leave a built-in unpinned, since the binary pins
its library. A configured provider whose tool is missing is a named skip
in the receipt, never an error: the machine not having a tool must not
fail the snapshot, it must be visible.

## The Ruby pair

**Prism** adds the call edges a lexical walk can see: a call whose
receiver is the enclosing class, and `new` on a written constant. Named
with no `command` it runs inside the binary and reads the index Rubydex
built in the same run, so it needs no Ruby. The reference script,
[`enola_prism_provider.rb`](https://github.com/enola-labs/enola/tree/main/examples/providers/ruby/prism) in enola's repository,
reads with Ruby's own parser on a Ruby 3.3 or newer; pin it to
`expected_version: "0.2.0"`. The two are close, not identical: the
built-in also writes the calls a class body makes (`validates`,
`before_action`), and writes the constant Rubydex resolved where the
script writes the one in the source.

**Rubydex** resolves constants through nesting and inheritance, types the
receiver of a call when it resolves to a constant, and linearises each
class's ancestry with mixins in resolution order. It runs inside the
binary against an engine library at the version enola pins: the install
script and `enola upgrade` fetch it, and after `pip install enola-cli`,
`go install` or a source build `enola providers fetch rubydex` does,
verifying the published checksum and caching it under your user cache
directory. `enola providers list` reports it. It indexes a tree with a
`Gemfile`; without one the census names the skip. It indexes the workspace and, when `bundle` is on PATH, the
gem paths the bundle reports, so a base class a gem declares resolves
(and the 357 view components under a gem's base class become a fact). No
gem enters your Gemfile.

Its facts carry their own resolution level, `resolved`, so a law can ask
for exactly them: the `ancestor:` component key reads the resolved
chain, and the `independent` form (a mixin never reaches its includers)
refuses by name without it.

## Signatures and the autoload map

Two more reference providers in enola's
[`examples/providers/ruby/`](https://github.com/enola-labs/enola/tree/main/examples/providers/ruby) read
what a Ruby tree declares rather than what it runs. Each is a plain-Ruby
script, pinned to its own `PROVIDER_VERSION` (`0.1.0` for both):

```yaml
providers:
  - name: rbs
    command: ["ruby", "/path/to/enola_rbs_provider.rb"]
    expected_version: "0.1.0"
  - name: zeitwerk
    command: ["ruby", "/path/to/enola_zeitwerk_provider.rb"]
    expected_version: "0.1.0"
```

- **rbs** reads RBS files, Sorbet `.rbi` files and inline `sig { }`
  blocks with a hand parser rather than the `rbs` gem, so its facts do not
  depend on which gem a machine has. It writes method contracts
  (`rbs-signature:`) and type declarations (`rbs-decl:`) at level
  `declared`, and the engine marks each extracted method a contract names
  `typed: true` with the files that declared it. A law can then require a
  declared signature on a public API. A declaration is a claim about the
  code, and the level says who made it.
- **zeitwerk** maps every file under an autoload root to the constant
  Zeitwerk expects it to define, from the path alone, without booting
  the app: `app/models/billing/invoice_item.rb` to
  `Billing::InvoiceItem`, concerns collapsed. Its facts are
  `convention-derived`. A path it cannot camelize with confidence (a
  dash, an uppercase letter) emits nothing and is counted, since without
  boot no inflector override is known.

## Reuse

Provider facts enter the same cache as the extractors' facts, so a
provider whose inputs did not move is not run again. A script whose
output partitions by file says so with `files: per-file` and the
`extensions:` it reads; enola then hands it only the files that
changed and keeps the rest. A provider that reads across files must not
declare that, because the cache would serve facts computed against a tree
that has since changed. The built-in Rubydex provider keeps one entry for
the whole index, keyed by the library version, the Ruby files with their
digests and `Gemfile.lock`, and rebuilds it on any change rather than
patching it. The receipt's `reuse` block says, per provider, what was
reused and what was computed, and for the index which part of the key did
not match.

## The census

Every provider states what it saw and what it skipped, and enola records
it per provider in the receipt:

```json
{"name": "rubydex", "version": "0.4.0", "fact_count": 666713,
 "census": {"files_seen": 43297, "declarations_parsed": 2698018,
            "constructs_skipped": 2244152,
            "skip_causes": [{"cause": "receiver resolves to no constant", "count": 1798420},
                            {"cause": "unresolved constant reference", "count": 28416}]}}
```

A skip has a cause; a provider never guesses. Read the census before
reading a verdict that surprises you.

## The runtime capture

The runtime provider reads captures an operator produced by running the
application: a booted-Rails capture (the final route table, reflected
associations, table bindings) and a query-counter capture (database
queries per frame under a spec run). Facts carry `runtime-observed` and
the channel they came from, and the engine cross-links them to the
measured ones. [`capture_spec_queries.rb`](https://github.com/enola-labs/enola/tree/main/examples/providers/ruby/runtime) in enola's
repository is the runner for the query capture: require it from
`spec_helper`, run the suite, and `.enola-runtime/queries.json` is written
with one frame per example. A `must_keep_budget metric: :queries, max: N`
law then verdicts on it, and refuses by name until a capture exists.

## Writing one

A provider is any program that prints JSONL facts in the store's schema
with a `resolution_level` on every fact and a prefix on every name so it
cannot collide with an extractor's identity, plus the one census line.
The Prism and eslint scripts in enola's
[`examples/providers/`](https://github.com/enola-labs/enola/tree/main/examples/providers) are the reference; each is under two hundred lines. Give it a `PROVIDER_VERSION`
it prints for `--version`, raise it whenever its facts change, and pin
that version in the configuration: a pin that no longer matches skips the
provider by name rather than mixing two versions' facts in one graph.

## Where next

- [A Rails application](02-rails.md): the Ruby pair in context, and the
  laws that need resolved ancestry.
- [Writing laws](04-writing-laws.md#when-a-law-refuses): what a law says
  when the provider it needs did not run.
- [Reading a verdict](20-reading-a-verdict.md#partial): why a provider
  present on one side only makes the verdict partial.

# Beyond one repository

A product is rarely one repository. enola indexes a cluster, several
repositories, into one union graph, links the seams between them (a
client's call matched to the route it reaches, a topic one publishes and
another consumes), and lets a law speak about them.

## The cluster

For a folder whose subfolders are the repositories, one command writes the
configuration:

```bash
enola cluster init ~/src/shop      # writes ~/src/shop/cluster.yaml
enola --generate ~/src/shop/cluster.yaml
```

A folder that is not itself a git repository and holds two or more of
them is indexed as a cluster without being asked: `--generate` and the
`generate_snapshot` tool say they detected the repositories, write
`cluster.yaml` there, and link them (`--no-cluster` indexes the folder as
one repository instead). Paths in the file resolve relative to it. When
the members do not share a folder, or the cluster carries settings of its
own, write the file yourself. Any name works, since you pass its path;
these guides call it `enola-cluster.yaml`, and
[`templates/enola-cluster.yaml`](../templates/enola-cluster.yaml) is one
to copy:

```yaml
# enola-cluster.yaml
repos:
  - ../backend
  - ../mobile
  - ../admin
  - .
ignore:
  - "**/node_modules/**"
  - "**/vendor/**"
  - "**/dist/**"
output:
  dir: .enola-cluster
providers:
  - name: rubydex
  - name: prism
```

```bash
enola --generate enola-cluster.yaml
```

Every repository's facts land in one store, labelled by repository, and
every member receives the whole union. Two things to know: **regenerate
the whole cluster, never one member**, since a snapshot scoped to one
repository replaces the union rather than updating its slice; and name
an output directory distinct from `.enola/`. The directory is resolved
inside each member (`backend/.enola-cluster`, `mobile/.enola-cluster`),
so with the default name the union overwrites each member's own
snapshot and the baseline pinned beside it.

## What the linker draws

- **Cross-repository dependencies**: a client's HTTP calls matched to a
  server's routes, GraphQL operations matched to a schema, shared code by
  import, each as a `repo -> repo` edge carrying the endpoints or imports
  that justify it.
- **Route coverage**: every server route marked as matched or unmatched by
  the loaded clients, and every client call marked as matched or unmatched
  by the loaded servers. A client call names the server routes it resolved
  to (`matched_routes`) and the symbol whose body makes it (`caller`), so
  "who calls this endpoint" is a query, and `enola endpoint 'GET
  /api/v2/orders' enola-cluster.yaml` asks it directly. In a Next.js or
  React client a call the app never sends is marked so, and a route whose
  every call is like that carries `unreached_by_clients`: called in the
  source, never sent.
- **What it missed**: `enola coverage` reports per service how many
  outbound calls it detected, resolved and left unresolved, and
  `--unresolved` lists each unresolved call with its file and line. An
  unresolved call is a repository you have not loaded, a third-party
  endpoint, or a blind spot; a service whose calls all go through an
  in-house wrapper reads as isolated until the wrapper is declared.
- **Declared seams**: a repository may declare what it consumes from
  another on a knowledge page, and the intent check verdicts the
  declaration against what was measured, refusing when the counterparty is
  absent.

## Your own HTTP client

When every call goes through something like
`http.sendRequest(serviceName, path, options)`, nothing says HTTP and the
calls are invisible. Declare the client in the configuration and the
TypeScript extractor reads its calls as client routes like any other:

```yaml
clients:
  - name: sdk-http
    language: typescript
    receiver_types: [IHttpRequestService]
    methods:
      - name: sendRequest
        service_arg: 0
        path_arg: 1
        options_arg: 2
        verb_option: method
        default_verb: GET

service_aliases:
  resource-api: gateway
```

A declaration teaches the extractor to read a call site; it never draws an
edge. The linker still links only to a loaded repository that serves the
path, and `service_aliases` only chooses among repositories that already
do. `linking.match_literal_against_params: true` lets a server path
parameter absorb a literal client segment, under conditions strict enough
that two candidate patterns match nothing. `service_aliases` and the
linking setting change the snapshot ID, so a baseline taken before either
is not comparable.

## Laws across the seam

```ruby
Enola.architecture "platform" do
  part :tables, files: "app/models/**", kind: :storage
  part :api, service: :backend, files: "config/**", kind: :route

  law "one owner per table" do
    tables.must_be_unique_across by: :table
    why "two writers to one table disagree in the end"
    mode :advisory
  end

  law "every api route has a consumer" do
    api.must_have_consumer
    why "a route nobody calls is a surface nobody maintains"
    mode :advisory
  end
end
```

`service:` scopes a part to one repository by its label. Both laws refuse
by name in a single-repository snapshot (`no_counterparty`): a table
nobody else could share is not unique, and a route with no client in a
snapshot that loaded no clients is not unconsumed. `forbid` between parts
in two services works with nothing new once the linker has drawn the edge.

## Grading the cluster

```bash
enola baseline pin enola-cluster.yaml
# change a member
enola --generate enola-cluster.yaml && enola check enola-cluster.yaml
```

A cluster baseline is comparable only when every member ran with the
same enola, the same providers and the same ignore globs; a member that
dropped out makes the pair incomparable and `check` declines, which is
the right answer when a whole repository's verdicts went quiet at once.

In CI that means checking out every member side by side, at the commits
under test, before generating; the [CI template](05-constraints-in-ci.md)
grades one repository, and these guides have no tested recipe for a
cluster yet. For an agent, `enola install --hooks` in the cluster's folder
installs only the steering hooks, since a baseline needs one repository
([hooks and agents](06-hooks-and-agents.md#the-hooks)); install inside
each member whose changes should be graded.

## The history

Every snapshot appends a revision to the architecture history under
`~/.enola/graphs`, so `enola log`, `enola blame` and `enola diff` answer
when a dependency entered the architecture and what the cluster looked
like at a date, and a law with `since "2026-08-01"` grades only the
breaches introduced after it (git dates a breach the history is too young
to know, as [writing laws](04-writing-laws.md) says). `enola history push` shares the record
through a directory store and `enola history pull` imports what other
machines pushed, so a team's machines agree on the past; with
`history.shared_dir` in the configuration the store can be left off both,
and `blame` and `diff` answer over the shared record. `history gc
--keep-last N` prints what it would prune from the shared store and
prunes only with `--apply`; `enola gc` does the same for the local one.
`history.dir` moves the local record, for instance into a directory you
commit.

## Where next

- [`examples/laws/cluster-laws`](../examples/laws/cluster-laws) and
  [`routes-have-consumers`](../examples/laws/routes-have-consumers): the
  laws above, ready to copy.
- [A knowledge base with enola](09-a-knowledge-base-with-enola.md): a
  twenty-repository cluster with decision pages anchored to its code.

# A knowledge base with enola

A team that keeps decisions beside its code (a wiki, ADRs, a design log)
can compile them into the graph. Then a file answers which decision
governs it, a decision answers which code it covers, a structural claim
in prose can be re-checked mechanically, and a finding judged once stays
judged. This guide is that practice, as it runs day to day on a
twenty-repository knowledge base.

> **An optional track.** Guides 09 to 12 are for a team that keeps
> decision records and wants each anchored to the code it governs. They
> assume enola set up as in [start here](01-start-here.md) and, for more
> than one repository, a [cluster](08-beyond-one-repo.md). Nothing in
> guides 01 to 08 needs them.
>
> They build the practice by hand, small enough to read and run without
> any tool of its own; [`examples/knowledge-base`](../examples/knowledge-base/README.md)
> is the smallest one the skills and hooks run against.
> [tabula](13-tabula.md), in preview and not yet public, is the same
> practice as one program.

## Pages compile into the graph

A markdown page carrying an `enola_intent:` block is an intent fact when
the snapshot is taken, and every anchor on it is an edge to a file:

```yaml
---
title: Charges run through one service
enola_intent:
  page:
    type: decision
    status: accepted
    scope:
      - shop
    relations:
      - rel: supersedes
        to: wiki/adrs/charges-in-controllers.md
    anchors:
      - repo: shop
        path: app/billing/charge.rb
      - repo: shop
        path: app/billing/refund.rb
---
```

Derive the block rather than hand-maintain it: if your pages already cite
the code they describe (`sources:` lines naming repository paths), the
anchors are those citations, and a small script stamps the block from
them and checks the derivation in CI. enola validates the block; keeping
it truthful to your conventions is yours.

Index the knowledge base as a member of the cluster, last, so its pages
compile over the code they anchor:

```yaml
repos:
  - ../shop
  - ../mobile
  - .
```

## Ask the graph what governs a file

```bash
enola plan -paths app/billing/charge.rb .
```

and over MCP, `governing_intent` for a file or a symbol: the pages whose
anchors cover it, with their relation trails (what supersedes what, what
depends on what), and for a page, which code its anchors cover. A file no
page governs is an answer too, and the difference between "no page
governs this" and "the graph was not asked" must stay visible: a missing
snapshot is a named skip, never silence.

This is the call behind the [intent-first gate](10-hooks.md): before an
agent's first edit into a repository, the governing pages are read.

## Laws over the pages

Because anchors are facts, laws can read them (see [writing
laws](04-writing-laws.md)):

```ruby
part :billing, files: "app/billing/**"
part :old_way, governed_by: "wiki/adrs/*.md status:superseded"
part :new_way, governed_by: "wiki/adrs/charges-in-one-service.md"

law "billing is documented" do
  billing.must_be_governed
  why "code under a decision needs the page that decided it"
end

law "the new way never reaches the old" do
  new_way.must_not_call :old_way
  why "a superseded decision's code is on its way out, not a dependency"
end
```

## Receipts are the committed state

Graph artifacts (`.enola/`, the cluster's output directory) are
machine-local and ignored. What enters version control is the receipt:
one entry per repository with the snapshot's fingerprint, the commit it
was taken at, the enola version and the providers that ran. Keep them in
one file the knowledge base owns:

```json
{"repos": {"shop": {"fingerprint": "…", "git_commit": "…", "enola_version": "0.4.35", "providers": ["prism", "rubydex"]}}}
```

Two rules from [beyond one repository](08-beyond-one-repo.md) matter
more here, because a page cites what the union said: regenerate the
whole cluster, never one member, and read a declined grade as "not
asked", never as clean.

## Citations with a grammar

A structural claim in prose ("`internal/facts` has 157 dependents")
cites the receipt it was read from, in one fixed shape, so a script can
re-check it against the committed receipts and flag the ones whose
digest moved. The shape is yours to choose; what matters is that there
is one, that one extractor parses it, and that a periodic sweep lists
every citation with a verdict (verified, stale, malformed). A claim
nobody can re-check is a sentence, not a fact.

## Findings are judged once

The explainers report candidates, not verdicts: a cycle at 0.7
confidence, a god class, an unused route. Before a finding grounds a
page, confirm it against the code and record the judgment in a ledger
beside the receipts, one entry per finding signature: accepted (and
where it landed), rejected, or permanent noise. The next session reads
the ledger instead of re-deciding, and the periodic sweep reports a
ledger entry whose finding no longer exists, which is the code moving
past a recorded judgment.

## Pulled, with one push

Skills fetch the graph while already reasoning about something: a
deepdive asks `impact_analysis` and `governing_intent`, an ingest checks
a claim with `query_facts` while the source is open, a drift sweep
regenerates and diffs receipts. Nothing lands on a board because the
graph said so. The one exception is the session-end hook, which speaks
only when the session's change introduced a structural regression, or
when it could not grade at all; a gate nobody remembers to run is no gate.

## The wrapper

Every skill calls a thin command the knowledge base owns rather than
the binary: `kb enola generate | receipt | diff | findings | judge | impact
| govern | citations | baseline | check | coverage | doctor`. It resolves
the binary, the cluster config and the receipts file, and when any is
absent it prints one line saying so and exits 0. That is what keeps a
skill from failing on a machine without enola, and what keeps "the graph
was not asked" distinguishable from "the graph agreed". The [wrapper
guide](12-the-wrapper.md) has its shape.

## Where next

[Knowledge-base hooks](10-hooks.md), then [the skills](11-the-skills-as-they-run.md)
and [the wrapper](12-the-wrapper.md) they call.

# Knowledge-base hooks: the graph at the moments that matter

A hook fires at a moment nobody has to remember: a session starting, the
first edit into a repository, a turn ending, a push. Each one here reads
the graph at that moment, blocks at most once, and forces a reading,
never a verdict. The scripts are in [`templates/hooks/`](../templates/hooks);
they are written for Claude Code's hook protocol (JSON on stdin, exit 2
to block with the message on stderr) and translate to any agent with
hooks.

Part of the [optional knowledge-base track](09-a-knowledge-base-with-enola.md):
these hooks hold an agent to a team's decision records. enola's own
session hooks, which pin a baseline and grade each turn in any
repository, come from `enola install --hooks` and are in
[hooks and agents](06-hooks-and-agents.md#the-hooks); install those first,
then these beside them.

What the four need:

- **A governed repository.** A repository is governed when one of
  `ENOLA_DECISION_DIRS` exists at its root (space-separated; default
  `wiki docs/decisions docs/adrs`). A Markdown file under one of them is a
  decision record; anything else in that repository is code. In a
  repository with none of those directories the gate, the record and the
  code-moved debt do nothing, so installing them globally is safe.
- `jq` on PATH for all four, and `python3` for the session refresh.
- For the session refresh, the knowledge base's receipts and cluster
  config ([guide 09](09-a-knowledge-base-with-enola.md)): `RECEIPTS`
  (default `wiki/_state/enola/receipts.json`) and `CLUSTER` (default
  `enola-cluster.yaml`).

Copy them into `.claude/hooks/`:

```bash
enola-guides copy hooks/intent-first-gate
enola-guides copy hooks/record
enola-guides copy hooks/stop-debt
enola-guides copy hooks/session-refresh
```

> With [tabula](13-tabula.md) (in preview, not yet public),
> `tabula install --harness claude` writes the gate, the record, the debt
> and the session hooks this guide wires by hand, and `--uninstall`
> removes exactly what it wrote. The hand-wired scripts below are the same
> ideas, short enough to read.

## The intent-first gate (PreToolUse on Edit and Write)

The first write into each repository per piece of work is blocked once.
The block carries two things: the pages that govern the file
(`governing_intent`, or `enola plan -paths <file>` when the MCP is not
in reach) and the pre-edit contract (the declared laws binding the path
and the blast radius over the current snapshot). The agent reads, then
retries, and the retry proceeds. The gate re-arms on every user message,
so each ask gets its own forced stop and no piece of work gets two.

What it refuses to do: decide. If the governing page contradicts the
intended change, the contract says amend the page first; the hook only
makes the page impossible to miss. When no page governs the file, it
says so and asks whether the work should be shaped. When the graph is
absent, it says so and lets the write through; a missing graph is a
named skip, never a wall.

`templates/hooks/intent-first-gate.sh` gates Edit and Write. The gate the
guides' author runs also classifies shell commands as writes (a `sed -i`, a
redirect, a `cp` into the repository); the template marks where that
classifier goes and leaves it out, because the rules for what counts as a
write depend on your tree.

## The stop-time debt (Stop)

When the turn ends, two debts can block it once each:

- **Code moved, no spec moved.** Files changed in a governed repository
  this turn and no decision record in it did. The block asks for either the
  amendment or an explicit sentence, in the reply, saying why the pages
  as written already cover the change.
- **A push went out with no grade.** A `git push` happened this turn and
  no `enola check` ran. This one applies in every repository. The block asks for the
  grade, read, before finishing.

Both read a small per-session record the PostToolUse hook writes
(`templates/hooks/record.sh`): which files moved, whether a push
happened, whether a check ran. The debt hook is the mechanical half of
two rules a team can otherwise only ask people to remember.

## The union refresh (SessionStart)

When the session starts, compare the paired repository's HEAD with the
commit the committed receipt records. When they differ, regenerate that
member's slice of the union in the background and say so in one line;
when they agree, say that. The agent's first structural question then
reads a graph that matches the checkout it is about to edit.

## Wiring

Claude Code, in `.claude/settings.json`, beside the entries
`enola install --hooks` wrote (it already registers `enola hook
session-start` and `enola hook stop`; do not add them a second time):

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [{"matcher": "startup|resume", "hooks": [
      {"type": "command", "command": "\"${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.}/.claude/hooks/session-refresh.sh\""}]}],
    "PreToolUse": [{"matcher": "Edit|Write|MultiEdit", "hooks": [
      {"type": "command", "command": "\"${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.}/.claude/hooks/intent-first-gate.sh\""}]}],
    "PostToolUse": [{"matcher": "Edit|Write|MultiEdit|Bash", "hooks": [
      {"type": "command", "command": "\"${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.}/.claude/hooks/record.sh\""}]}],
    "UserPromptSubmit": [{"hooks": [
      {"type": "command", "command": "\"${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.}/.claude/hooks/record.sh\" reset"}]}],
    "Stop": [{"hooks": [
      {"type": "command", "command": "\"${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-.}/.claude/hooks/stop-debt.sh\""}]}]
  }
}
```

## What it feels like

An agent asked to change a billing service edits nothing until it has
read the decision that put charges through one service; it grades the
change before the push and writes the grade into the pull request; and
when it ends the turn having changed code under a decision without
touching the decision, it is asked to account for that once. None of
this needs the agent to know enola exists.

## Where next

[The knowledge-base skills](11-the-skills-as-they-run.md), which these
hooks enforce, and [the wrapper](12-the-wrapper.md) they call.

# The knowledge-base skills, as they run

A skill is a named piece of practice an agent follows. Each of these asks
the graph one specific question at one specific moment; the value is the
moment, not the prompt. They are described here as they run on a
twenty-repository knowledge base, and shipped under
[`templates/skills/`](../templates/skills) to copy. They call the
knowledge base's [wrapper](12-the-wrapper.md), not the binary, so install
it first. Part of the [optional knowledge-base track](09-a-knowledge-base-with-enola.md);
the four skills for any repository are in
[hooks and agents](06-hooks-and-agents.md#the-skill).

> With [tabula](13-tabula.md) (in preview, not yet public), one `tabula`
> skill and the loop it runs (search, claim, govern, align, impact,
> baseline, grade, report, release) take the place of the five skills
> below; they stay here as the practice written out.

## Before shaping work: the deepdive (`enola-deepdive`)

Shaping a change starts with three graph questions, answered before a
line of the plan is written:

- `impact_analysis` on every symbol the work would change: fan-in,
  fan-out, named callers. A symbol with 157 dependents is a different
  plan from one with 3.
- `governing_intent` on the paths: which decisions already cover the
  area, so the plan amends a page rather than contradicting it.
- `query_insights` for the area: what the explainers already computed (a
  cycle someone must have introduced, a layer crossed, a dead route), so
  the plan inherits judged findings instead of rediscovering them.

The plan cites the receipt it read from, so a later reader can re-check
the numbers.

## Before building: the grade (`enola-grade-before-push`)

`set_baseline` once, early; after the change, `generate_snapshot` and
`diff_snapshot`; the delta (introduced, resolved, edges added) goes into
the pull request in one sentence. A declined comparison is not a pass.
This is also the [stop-time debt](10-hooks.md) hook's demand.

## While ingesting a source: the claim check (`enola-ingest-check`)

A page that states a structural fact (a stack, a public surface, a
route, a table) checks it while the source is open: `query_facts` for
the fact, `impact_analysis` for the count. A wrong claim ingested today
is cited by a page tomorrow and reasoned from by an agent next week, so
verification is cheapest now. For an incremental ingest, each changed
path runs through `governing_intent`: the pages whose anchors cover a
changed file are exactly the synthesis that may have drifted, and a
changed file no page governs is a gap the ingest may be about to fill.

## The periodic sweep: drift (`enola-drift`)

On a schedule, or before publishing: regenerate the cluster, diff the
committed receipts (fingerprint and commit per member), and read
`coverage_report` for which cross-repository edges resolved and which did
not. Receipts that moved name the members whose pages want a re-read.
Not a comparison of findings between two runs; that is the grade's job.

## Knowledge hygiene: citations and the ledger (`enola-citation-hygiene`)

Every receipt citation in prose gets a verdict against the committed
receipts: verified, stale (the digest moved), malformed. Stale ones are
re-read, not rewritten. The finding ledger is swept the same way: an
accepted finding whose evidence no longer exists in the graph is the
code moving past a judgment, and the page that cites it is re-read.

## Stepping back: the blast radius (`enola-zoom-out`)

When deep in a change, one call answers how it sits in the whole:
`impact_analysis` for the symbols in hand, `find_path` between the
part being changed and the parts that consume it, `governing_intent`
for the decisions around it. The answer is one paragraph of technical
fit the agent can stand on, beside the product fit it reasons out.

## Writing and explaining laws (`enola-laws`)

Covered in [writing laws](04-writing-laws.md): lint before verdict,
`constraints explain` before arguing with a verdict, ratchet before
strict.

## What makes these skills and not prompts

Each names the call, the moment, and the refusal: what the agent does
when the graph is absent (say so, proceed, never pretend), when the
comparison declines (re-pin, never read as clean), when a finding is a
candidate (confirm against the code, judge once, record). The
[hooks](10-hooks.md) enforce these rules; the skills explain them.

## Where next

[The wrapper](12-the-wrapper.md) every one of these skills calls.

# The wrapper

Skills call a command the knowledge base owns, not the binary. The
wrapper is thin: it knows where the binary, the cluster config and the
receipts file live, it records receipts after a generate, and when
anything is absent it prints one line saying so and exits 0. That is the
whole design, and it is what lets every skill run on a machine without
enola without failing, while keeping "the graph was not asked" a
different sentence from "the graph agreed".

[`templates/kb/kb`](../templates/kb/kb) is one, in Python 3 with the
standard library only. From the knowledge base's root:

```bash
enola-guides copy templates/kb     # writes bin/kb; put bin/ on PATH
kb enola doctor
```

It reads three settings from the environment: `ENOLA_BIN` (the binary,
default `enola` on PATH), `KB_CLUSTER` (the cluster config, default
`enola-cluster.yaml`, else `cluster.yaml`) and `KB_KNOWLEDGE` (the pages
directory, default `wiki`; receipts go in
`wiki/_state/enola/receipts.json` and the ledger in `findings.json`
beside them). [`examples/knowledge-base`](../examples/knowledge-base/README.md)
is a knowledge base it runs against. Part of the
[optional knowledge-base track](09-a-knowledge-base-with-enola.md).

> With [tabula](13-tabula.md) there is no wrapper to write: `govern`,
> `impact` and `evaluate` ask the engine themselves and say "not asked"
> rather than pass, which is the named skip this guide builds.

## The operations

| Op | Answers |
|---|---|
| `generate` | snapshot the cluster, then record every member's receipt |
| `receipt [member]` | what was recorded |
| `diff` | which members' live receipts drifted from the recorded ones |
| `findings [--repo] [--all]` | the explainers' findings across the cluster, attributed to the member their evidence names, with judged ones hidden |
| `judge <signature> accepted\|rejected\|noise [--reason TEXT] [--landed PAGE]` | record a verdict in the ledger |
| `impact <symbol>` | fan-in, fan-out, named callers, read from the on-disk facts |
| `govern <path or page>` | the pages governing a file, or the code a page anchors |
| `citations` | every receipt citation in prose with its verdict |
| `baseline pin\|show\|clear [member]` | the "before" a change is graded against |
| `check [member]` | the grade, reported, never gating |
| `coverage` | which cross-repository edges resolved |
| `doctor` | whether the hooks fire |

## The shape, in any language

The template is this, and a wrapper of your own in another language keeps
the same branches:

```
resolve binary   -> absent: print "enola: not installed, the graph was not asked"; exit 0
resolve config   -> absent: print the path looked for; exit 0
resolve receipts -> absent on a read op: print; exit 0
run the op       -> on generate, read each member's .enola/receipt.json
                    and write fingerprint, commit, version, providers
                    into the receipts file
exit codes       -> the binary's, except check: report, exit 0
```

Three things to keep:

- **Receipts are the only committed state.** `generate` writes them;
  nothing else does. `diff` compares them to the live ones; it is not a
  comparison of findings.
- **Findings read from disk, not the MCP server.** `impact` and
  `findings` parse the fact and insight files, so scheduled and headless
  runs keep working when no server is up.
- **`check` reports; it never gates.** The binary exits 1 on a
  regression and the wrapper does not propagate it: no graph-dependent
  step may stop work, so the verdict is surfaced for a person to weigh.
  Exit 3 from the binary means the snapshots were not comparable; the
  wrapper prints that as "not asked", never as a pass.

A citation in prose has one grammar, `receipt <member>@<commit>,
fingerprint <4 hex>…<4 hex>` (`receipt rails-shop@3f2a9c1, fingerprint
8d1e…c40a`), and `citations` reports anything else that starts
`receipt X@` as malformed. Members are labelled by their directory name.

## The ledger beside the receipts

```json
{"findings": {"constraints|Constraint background-jobs-never-invoke-controller-code violated: ReceiptJob#perform -> OrdersController via calls": {"verdict": "accepted", "at": "2026-08-22", "reason": "real; the receipt renders through the controller", "landed": "wiki/shop/permanent/architecture.md"}}}
```

One entry per finding signature, `<explainer>|<title>`, written on
judgment. There is no
pending state: unjudged findings are observations, not a to-do list, and
nothing enumerates them as work.

## Why not call the binary directly

Every skill would then carry the absent-binary branch, the config
resolution and the receipt bookkeeping, and they would drift. The
wrapper is where those live once, which is why the skills say
`kb enola impact` and never a path to the binary.

## Where next

[tabula](13-tabula.md), in preview: the same practice as one program.

# tabula: the knowledge base, kept by a tool

> **Preview.** tabula is not public yet: the links to its repository and
> releases will not open until it is, and nothing else in these guides
> needs it. This guide is here so the practice it describes can be read
> ahead of the release.

Guides 09 to 12 build a knowledge base by hand: pages anchored to code, a
wrapper, four hooks, five skills, receipts and a ledger. [tabula](https://github.com/misabegovic/tabula)
is that practice as one program. It keeps the pages, checks them against
a contract, compiles their laws into enola constraints, grades a plan
against the code with enola, and holds every agent that works on the
code to the page that governs it. This guide is what an enola user needs
to know to start; tabula's own documentation under `docs/wiki/` goes
further, and every verb prints the command to run next and why.

## What it adds to enola

enola measures what the code is and grades what a change did to it.
tabula holds what the code should be, in pages a person writes:

- **Architecture pages** (`.tabula`, `kind: architecture`) draw parts and
  arrows and state laws as sentences; `tabula architecture --write`
  compiles them into `enola/constraints/` in the repository, so the
  repository's own `enola check` enforces them with no tabula in CI.
- **PRDs** (`kind: initiative`) carry acceptance bullets, each settled by
  an observation: a test to run, a count over the facts, or
  `grade: enola check clean`. `tabula evaluate` settles every bullet as
  met, not met, not checked or does not apply, with no model involved,
  and writes the verdict into the decision record beside the PRD with a
  receipt.
- **The loop**: search before reading, claim before working, find the
  governing page before editing, grade before finishing, report what
  happened. Hooks refuse an edit until the agent has recorded the page it
  is working from.

## Install

A tabula release carries cardo inside the binary: a build derived from
enola by tabula's author, the engine tabula is developed against. Download the archive for your platform from
the [releases](https://github.com/misabegovic/tabula/releases), check it
against `SHA256SUMS`, and put `tabula` on your PATH:

```bash
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
tar -xzf tabula-0.0.1-linux-amd64.tar.gz
install -m 755 tabula-0.0.1-linux-amd64/tabula ~/.local/bin/tabula
tabula doctor
```

v0.0.1 is built for linux-amd64 only. On any other platform, build from a
clone with `cargo build --release` (the repository pins its Rust
toolchain); a plain build carries no engine and uses the one on your PATH.

tabula looks for an engine in this order: `engine.binary` in
`tabula.config.yml`, then `cardo`, `cardo-current` and `enola` on your
PATH, and only then the cardo it carries, which it unpacks into its cache
the first time a verb needs it and checks against its digest. So an
`enola` you installed for the other guides is the engine tabula runs,
with a warning on every line that carries its result. `tabula doctor` says which engine answered and how it
was found (`engine` and `carried` lines); set `engine.binary` to choose
one, or `engine.carried: never` to leave the carried copy out. tabula
never installs or upgrades an engine of its own accord.

## The first run

```bash
mkdir shop-brain && cd shop-brain
tabula init --tour
tabula tour
```

`init --tour` writes an empty project (a `wiki/`, an `AGENTS.md` stating
the contract, `tabula.config.yml`) and a small inherited shop with the
facts an engine already read from it, so the tour runs without one.
`tabula tour` names the one command to run next, read off the project
each time: write a page, find it with `search`, `explain` the shop from
its facts, `picture` its architecture page, then `evaluate` a PRD the
shop does not meet yet, fix one line, and evaluate it again.

For your own code, name the repositories in `tabula.config.yml`
(`projects_root`, `active_repos`) and let the engine draft a first page:

```bash
tabula explain shop --generate
```

writes a page a newcomer can read, every sentence a claim with its file
and line, and, when the repository has no architecture page yet, a draft
at `wiki/shop/architecture/explained.tabula` that forbids nothing.

## Laws, from a page to `enola check`

```bash
tabula say shop/architecture/shop.tabula "orders never calls gateway." \
  --because "billing alone talks to the payment gateway."
tabula architecture shop/architecture/shop.tabula --write
```

`say` writes the law under the page's `***laws***` and reads it back with
what the code shows today, a count and never a verdict. `--write` puts
the compiled rules in the repository:

```yaml
# enola/constraints/shop.yaml
# Compiled by `tabula architecture` from the page `shop/architecture/shop.tabula`; edit the page, not this file.
components:
  - name: orders
    match: ["shop/orders.py"]
  - name: gateway
    match: ["shop/gateway.py"]
rules:
  # orders never calls gateway.
  - id: orders-never-calls-gateway
    forbid: orders
    to: gateway
    via: calls
    mode: ratchet
    since: 2026-10-25
    because: >-
      billing alone talks to the payment gateway.
```

That file is plain enola YAML, and upstream enola v0.4.35 lints it clean.
Commit it in the repository and grade it there exactly as
[constraints in CI](05-constraints-in-ci.md) describes. A sentence with no
strength word is `ratchet`; `, as a warning.` is `advisory` and
`, without exception.` is `strict`. A rule no sentence can say is written
in enola's own form under `laws/` at the project root, and `tabula
export` copies it into the repository with the compiled pages.

## A plan graded against the code

```text
***specs***

- An order's total counts every line, discounts included.

  ***acceptance***

  - A discount line lowers the total.
    test: ~/projects/shop/tests/test_totals.py -- python3 -B -m unittest tests.test_totals
  - The change crosses no law.
    grade: enola check clean
```

`tabula evaluate shop/prds/totals-add-up.tabula` runs the test and asks the
engine for `check --json --fail-on=constraints` on every repository the
PRD anchors. A regression, whole or partial, is not met; no baseline,
incomparable snapshots or no engine is "not checked", never a pass. A
bullet not met exits 5, and the fix is in the code: tabula's rule is that
the bullet, its observation and the checked block are never edited to
make a verdict pass.

## Agents

```bash
tabula install --harness claude      # or agents, pi, codex
```

opens tabula's doors to one harness: for Claude Code, hooks in
`.claude/settings.json`, a `tabula` MCP server in `.mcp.json` and a
skill, each file recorded in `wiki/_state/install.json` so `--uninstall`
removes exactly what it wrote. The `agents` harness covers anything that
reads `AGENTS.md` (opencode, goose, Cline, OpenHands, Amp). tabula's
repository is also a Claude Code plugin marketplace, under
`editors/claude-code`, carrying the same server, hooks and skill plus the
`.tabula` language server.

The skill's rule is one line: search before reading, claim before
working, evaluate before finishing. The loop it runs is
`tabula run loop --flow`: search, claim, find the governing page with
`govern`, record it with `align` (or write the intent first), check the
blast radius with `impact`, pin a baseline, edit from the aligned
bullets, grade, report, release. The edit gate refuses a write until
`align` has recorded the page the change is generated from, and a write
from the shell is caught by git's status, not by reading the command.

tabula's hooks and enola's (`enola install --hooks`) do different jobs
and sit side by side in `.claude/settings.json`: enola's pin a baseline,
grade the session and turn the first searches toward the graph; tabula's
hold the agent to the page. Install enola's first. In v0.4.34, running
`enola install --hooks` again after tabula's were in place added enola's
stop hook a second time, inside tabula's stop entry, so the session was
graded twice per turn. After re-running it, check `.claude/settings.json`
holds one `enola hook stop`, and remove a copy if it holds two.

## Which hand-built piece tabula replaces

| Guides 09 to 12 | With tabula |
|---|---|

# taha: agents under a mandate

> **Preview.** taha is not public yet: the links to its repository and
> releases will not open until it is, and nothing else in these guides
> needs it. This guide is here so the practice it describes can be read
> ahead of the release.

[taha](https://github.com/misabegovic/taha), short for tabula harness, is a
command-line tool that runs coding agents on a [tabula](13-tabula.md)
project and keeps them on track. You say what you want; taha routes it
through tabula's intent pages (a pitch, a plan, a decision record, then
the build), runs the agent, settles routine questions with a council of
reviewers, and stops to ask you before anything is published. taha
decides nothing tabula can decide: every gate it applies is a tabula
verdict, and a bug in taha can at worst stop a run, never let a failed
check through.

This guide is where taha meets enola. taha's own
[first hour](https://github.com/misabegovic/taha/blob/main/docs/first-hour.md)
fixes one bug in a sample project in ten stops with no model and no
account, and [the menu](https://github.com/misabegovic/taha/blob/main/docs/menu.md)
lists every command by goal; start there.

## Install

taha is not on npm yet, and the name `taha` on npm belongs to another
package, so `npm install -g taha` installs something else. Install from a
clone, with Node 22.19 or newer, on Linux or macOS (Windows through WSL):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/misabegovic/taha && cd taha
npm install
npm link
taha help
```

taha runs the tabula `TABULA_BIN` names, else the newer of the tabula its
platform package carries and the one on your PATH. A clone has no platform
package, so [install tabula](13-tabula.md#install) first.

## What a run is

One piece of work, an issue or a PRD slug, is one durable conversation
kept in SQLite under `state/`, so a crash or a restart never repeats an
act. The run claims the piece with `tabula claim`, attaches `tabula serve`
over the project, and journals every committed step into the project's
journal. Before a piece can finish `done` or open a pull request,
`tabula evaluate` must read every acceptance bullet met; a PRD bullet
written as `grade: enola check clean` is how enola's verdict becomes one
of them.

What the run may do is written in a mandate, `wiki/mandates/default.md`:
the acts it may take (`allow`, `ask`, `never`), its budget, whether it is
`supervised` or `autonomous`, the repositories in scope, the test command,
and when it expires. GitHub is reached through one connector whose only
writes are a branch, a push, a draft pull request and a comment; each is
journaled before it runs, a pull request is always a draft, and taha has
no way to mark one ready or merge it. Anything public waits in the inbox
for you:

```bash
taha                       # what runs, what waits on you, what is next
taha approve <finding>     # a yes to what waits
taha steer <run> <words>   # change a run in flight
taha stop <run>            # stop at the next safe point
```

## Adopting a repository that enola already measures

```bash
cd ~/src/shop
taha adopt --inside        # or --beside --repo shop, to write nothing into it
taha doctor
```

`adopt --inside` adds the project's files to the repository, records the
repository's own checks so a push waits for them, and, for the code map,
writes `mcp-arch.yaml` and runs `cardo --generate` in the repository.
`adopt --beside` writes nothing into the repository and leaves the
snapshot to you. `taha doctor` prints one line each for the layout, the
mandate, the state folder, the schedule and the code map, and exits 0
when all of them read `ready`.

taha calls the engine as `cardo`, by that name on your PATH; it does not
fall back to `enola`. The cardo a [tabula release](13-tabula.md#install)
carries is unpacked into tabula's cache, and `tabula doctor` prints where
(the `engine` line). Until cardo has an install of its own, link that copy
onto your PATH for taha:

```bash
ln -s "$HOME/.cache/tabula/engine/<digest>/cardo" ~/.local/bin/cardo
```

An `mcp-arch.yaml` the repository already has is left as it is, so the
providers [guide 02](02-rails.md#the-two-providers) configures keep
running.

## Where enola's laws stay

taha adds no law of its own. The laws are the repository's
`enola/constraints/`, written by hand or compiled from tabula's
architecture pages, and they are graded by the repository's CI with
`enola check` as [guide 05](05-constraints-in-ci.md) describes, whoever
or whatever wrote the change. taha's part is to make an agent's run reach
that CI only as a draft, after tabula's checks, with you asked first.

## Where next

[Constraints in CI](05-constraints-in-ci.md): the check every change
reaches, whoever wrote it.

# A Python service

What enola measures in a Python codebase, the laws a Python team states,
and the one place the shipped recipes need a hand. The worked example is
[`examples/python-service`](../examples/python-service): a FastAPI
service in four packages that breaks three laws on purpose, snapshotted
by CI on every change to this repository.

## Install

```bash
pipx install enola-cli       # or: uv tool install enola-cli; the command is enola
enola --version
```

`enola` was taken on PyPI, so the project is `enola-cli`; it is the same
binary as the install script and the GitHub release. Install it as a
tool, outside your project's environment; a bare `pip install` into the
system Python is refused on current Debian and Ubuntu. Pin it with
`enola-cli==0.4.35` when you need the release these guides were checked
against. Then the loop from [start here](01-start-here.md):

```bash
enola --explain .
enola --generate .
enola baseline pin .
```

## What enola measures

A tree is Python when it carries `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py`,
`requirements.txt`, `Pipfile` or one of the tool configs, at the root or
up to three levels down. Parsed with tree-sitter, never imported:

- **Modules are directories.** `shop/api` and `shop/domain` are modules;
  a law's `match:` globs select files, and the module edges between
  directories are what cycles and layers read.
- **Imports** are `imports` edges, each tagged `internal`, `external` or
  `stdlib`. Calls are `calls` edges from a function to what it calls,
  with the calls made inside a loop recorded on the caller for N+1
  hunting.
- **Routes** from FastAPI and Flask, at their composed runtime path:
  `include_router(r, prefix="/p")` folds `/p` onto every route `r`
  declares, across files.
- **Storage** from SQLAlchemy models, each with its table name.
- **Module-level code** (what runs at import time) is kept on a
  `file_ref`, an edge carrier rather than architecture.
- **Tests** (`tests/`, `test_*.py`, `conftest.py`) are reference-only.

What it leaves out on purpose: a route whose path is not a literal, a
mount with a computed prefix (its routes keep their bare paths), routes a
plugin registers at import time, and dispatch through `getattr`.

## The laws

The `layered` recipe names four roles. Bind them to your packages:

```yaml
use_recipe:
  - recipe: layered
    as: shop
    mode: ratchet
    bind:
      presentation: { match: ["shop/api/**"] }
      application: { match: ["shop/services/**"] }
      domain: { match: ["shop/domain/**"] }
      infrastructure: { match: ["shop/repositories/**"] }
```

Its three rules over `calls` hold on Python as written: the API reaches
the services only, services never call back into the API, repositories
never drive the services (`infrastructure-does-not-drive-the-domain`,
which despite its name forbids infrastructure calling the application
layer). In the example, a route that reads a
repository directly breaks the first one:

```text
Constraint shop/presentation-reaches-application-only violated: shop/api/orders.list_recent -> shop/repositories/orders.recent_orders via calls
```

**Its two domain rules read `depends_on`, and Python's extractor writes
`imports`,** so on a Python tree they are silent whatever the domain
imports. `via:` names one edge kind exactly ([writing laws](04-writing-laws.md#recipes)
says why). State the domain's law over the edge Python has:

```yaml
components:
  - name: domain
    match: ["shop/domain/**"]
  - name: storage
    match: ["shop/repositories/**"]
rules:
  - id: the-domain-imports-no-storage
    forbid: domain
    to: storage
    via: imports
    mode: ratchet
    because: "The domain is the part that outlives the database; a domain that imports a table cannot be tested or reasoned about without it."
```

```text
Constraint the-domain-imports-no-storage violated: module-edge: shop/domain -> shop/repositories -> shop/repositories via imports
```

`ports-and-adapters`, `clean` and `modular-monolith` are the other
arrangements enola ships; read which `via:` each rule names before
binding one, and run `enola constraints lint .` after a snapshot to see
what every part resolved to.

## Dependencies

Each direct dependency in `pyproject.toml` or `requirements.txt` is a
fact (`pkg:pypi/fastapi`), pinned when the constraint is `==` or a
lockfile resolves it. The `supply-chain` recipe is the law that every one
is pinned:

```yaml
use_recipe:
  - recipe: supply-chain
    as: supply
    mode: ratchet
    bind:
      unpinned-dependencies: {}
```

```text
Constraint supply/dependencies-are-pinned violated: pkg:pypi/fastapi is measured in supply/unpinned-dependencies
```

## Explainers worth gating on

- **`import-closure`** answers what `import shop` actually executes,
  including the `__init__.py` files no import names, and names the
  initialisations responsible for most of it: a barrel written for
  convenience that makes importing the public API load a scraping
  library. The barrels it names are gateable with
  `-fail-on import-closure`.
- **`query-loops`** reports a call that reaches storage inside a loop
  over input, the N+1 candidates.
- **`cycles`** between packages, which Python allows and an import at
  function scope hides from a reader.

For CI, [constraints in CI](05-constraints-in-ci.md) and enola-action
apply unchanged; the Rubydex step is for Ruby and can be dropped.

## Where next

- [Writing laws](04-writing-laws.md): every sentence, the modes, and the
  carve-outs.
- [Constraints in CI](05-constraints-in-ci.md): the check on every pull
  request.
- [Rolling out](19-rolling-out.md): adopting it on a codebase that already
  breaks the laws you want.
- [Reading a verdict](20-reading-a-verdict.md): every section of the
  output.

# A TypeScript or JavaScript service

What enola measures in a TypeScript or JavaScript codebase, the laws a
Node team states, and the two places the code's shape decides what a law
can see. The worked example is
[`examples/typescript-service`](../examples/typescript-service): an
Express service in four directories that breaks three laws on purpose,
snapshotted by CI on every change to this repository. Front ends have a
guide of their own for Ember ([guide 03](03-ember.md)); Angular, Vue,
Nuxt, Svelte and Next.js are read by the same extractor.

## Install

enola is not on npm, and the npm package named `enola` is an unrelated
tool that deletes files: do not `npm install -g enola`. Install the
binary once per machine:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/enola-labs/enola/main/install.sh | sh
enola --version
```

or `pipx install enola-cli`, or a binary from the
[releases](https://github.com/enola-labs/enola/releases) for Linux, macOS
and Windows. Then the loop from [start here](01-start-here.md).

## What enola measures

- **Modules are directories**; `import … from` is an `imports` edge,
  tagged `internal` or `external`, and a call is a `calls` edge from the
  function that makes it.
- **Server routes** from Express (mounts composed across files), NestJS
  (controller prefixes composed), InversifyJS, and file-based routing in
  Next.js, Nuxt and SvelteKit.
- **Client calls** (`fetch`, axios, Angular's `HttpClient`, a wrapper
  another file exports) as client routes, which the cluster linker
  matches to a server's routes ([guide 08](08-beyond-one-repo.md)); an
  in-house client is declared under `clients:`.
- **Storage** from Prisma, TypeORM and Drizzle, each with its physical
  table name; a Drizzle query flags the function doing I/O.
- **GraphQL** operations and schema-first servers, **Kafka** and AsyncAPI
  contracts.

## The laws

Bind the `layered` recipe to your directories:

```yaml
use_recipe:
  - recipe: layered
    as: shop
    mode: ratchet
    bind:
      presentation: { match: ["src/routes/**"] }
      application: { match: ["src/services/**"] }
      domain: { match: ["src/domain/**"] }
      infrastructure: { match: ["src/db/**"] }
```

```text
Constraint shop/presentation-reaches-application-only violated: src/routes.listRecent -> src/db.recentOrders via calls
```

**A handler's calls belong to the handler only when it has a name.** An
inline arrow, `router.get("/recent", async (req, res) => …)`, puts its
calls on the file's `file_ref`, which the edge rules do not walk, so the
same breach written inline reports nothing. Name the handler (an
exported function the router registers) and the route also carries a
`handled_by` edge to it, which is what `enola endpoint` and the
route-scoped laws follow.

**The recipe's two domain rules read `depends_on`, and the TypeScript
extractor writes `imports`,** so they are silent on a TypeScript tree
([writing laws](04-writing-laws.md#recipes) says why). State the domain's
law over imports:

```yaml
components:
  - name: domain
    match: ["src/domain/**"]
  - name: storage
    match: ["src/db/**"]
rules:
  - id: the-domain-imports-no-storage
    forbid: domain
    to: storage
    via: imports
    mode: ratchet
    because: "The domain is the part that outlives the database; a domain that imports a schema cannot be tested or reasoned about without it."
```

```text
Constraint the-domain-imports-no-storage violated: src/domain -> src/db/schema -> src/db/schema via imports
```

In v0.4.35 an Express `router.post("/", …)` mounted at `/orders`
produces no route, while `router.post("/create", …)` comes out as
`POST /orders/create`; a law or a coverage count over a router's root
path does not see it yet.

## Dependencies

Each direct dependency in `package.json` is a fact (`pkg:npm/express`),
pinned when its constraint is one exact version or `package-lock.json` or
`yarn.lock` resolves it. A `pnpm-lock.yaml` or `bun.lockb` beside the
manifest leaves `pinned` absent, since enola cannot read it, and a law
over `pinned` then says nothing rather than something false. The example
has no lockfile, so its `^4.19.2` is a breach of `supply-chain`:

```text
Constraint supply/dependencies-are-pinned violated: pkg:npm/express is measured in supply/unpinned-dependencies
```

## A provider of your own

eslint's findings join the graph through the reference provider in
enola's `examples/providers/js/eslint/`, a Node script under two hundred
lines that reads the results file your lint step writes; configure it as
[providers](07-providers.md) shows.

## Where next

- [Writing laws](04-writing-laws.md): every sentence, the modes, and the
  carve-outs.
- [Constraints in CI](05-constraints-in-ci.md): the check on every pull
  request.
- [Rolling out](19-rolling-out.md): adopting it on a codebase that already
  breaks the laws you want.
- [Reading a verdict](20-reading-a-verdict.md): every section of the
  output.

# A Go service

What enola measures in a Go codebase, and the laws worth writing where
the compiler already forbids an import cycle. The worked example is
[`examples/go-service`](../examples/go-service): a chi service in four
packages that breaks two laws on purpose, snapshotted by CI on every
change to this repository.

## Install

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/enola-labs/enola/main/install.sh | sh
enola --version
```

enola is written in Go, and a source build is `go install ./cmd/enola`
from a clone of [enola-labs/enola](https://github.com/enola-labs/enola),
with Go 1.26 or newer and a C compiler for the tree-sitter bindings. The
prebuilt binary needs neither. Then the loop from
[start here](01-start-here.md).

## What enola measures

- **Packages are modules**, imports are `imports` edges between them, and
  calls are `calls` edges from the function that makes them, including a
  function used as a value (a dispatch-table entry, a callback).
- **Routes** from `net/http`, gin, chi and the other routers, with prefixes
  composed across function boundaries; outbound HTTP calls as client
  routes; gRPC and Kafka on both sides.
- **Loops**: a call made inside a loop over input is recorded on the
  caller, which is what `query-loops` reads for N+1 candidates.
- **Multi-module repositories**: imports resolve through every `go.mod`
  in the repository, so a monorepo with one module per service, or a
  module nested in another, gets internal edges between them rather than
  external, unresolved ones.

## The laws

Go's compiler refuses an import cycle between packages, so gating on
`cycles` enforces what the toolchain enforces first. The laws a Go team
needs are the ones no compiler states: which package may reach which.

```yaml
use_recipe:
  - recipe: layered
    as: shop
    mode: ratchet
    bind:
      presentation: { match: ["internal/web/**"] }
      application: { match: ["internal/checkout/**"] }
      domain: { match: ["internal/order/**"] }
      infrastructure: { match: ["internal/store/**"] }
```

```text
Constraint shop/presentation-reaches-application-only violated: internal/web.listRecent -> internal/store.RecentOrders via calls
```

**The recipe's two domain rules read `depends_on`, and Go's extractor
writes `imports`,** so they are silent on a Go tree
([writing laws](04-writing-laws.md#recipes) says why). State the domain's
law over imports:

```yaml
components:
  - name: domain
    match: ["internal/order/**"]
  - name: storage
    match: ["internal/store/**"]
rules:
  - id: the-domain-imports-no-storage
    forbid: domain
    to: storage
    via: imports
    mode: ratchet
    because: "The domain is the part that outlives the database; a domain package that imports the store cannot be tested or reasoned about without it."
```

```text
Constraint the-domain-imports-no-storage violated: internal/order -> example.com/shop/internal/store -> internal/store via imports
```

Go's own `internal/` rule stops another module importing your internals;
a `forbid` between two of your own `internal/` packages is the rule it
leaves to you.

## Dependencies

A `require` in `go.mod` names an exact version, so every direct
dependency is pinned and `supply-chain` holds; the example binds it and
it reports that its part matches nothing. `// indirect` lines are the
closure and are not read.

## Where next

- [Writing laws](04-writing-laws.md): every sentence, the modes, and the
  carve-outs.
- [Constraints in CI](05-constraints-in-ci.md): the check on every pull
  request.
- [Rolling out](19-rolling-out.md): adopting it on a codebase that already
  breaks the laws you want.
- [Reading a verdict](20-reading-a-verdict.md): every section of the
  output.
